Owen v. Cohen (Cal. 1941)

Source: casebook p. 355 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: In a bowling-alley partnership, one partner tried to dominate, humiliated the other, refused to work, and took money without consent.

Held: Court-ordered dissolution affirmed; persistent misconduct destroying cooperation is enough. The other partner's loan is repaid first from the sale.

Why it matters: Grounds for judicial dissolution (now RUPA § 801(4)).

supplemental reading

Page v. Page (Cal. 1961)

Source: casebook p. 364 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: Two brothers' linen partnership lost money for years; once it turned profitable, the brother whose company held its debt sought to dissolve it.

Held: It was an at-will partnership, so he may dissolve — but only in good faith; he may not freeze out his brother to grab the business.

Why it matters: The good-faith limit on dissolution and how to tell at-will from term partnerships.

main case

Creel v. Lilly (Md. 1999)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 403.

Facts: After a partner died, the survivors inventoried and valued the store and paid his estate its share; the widow demanded a full liquidation sale.

Held: No forced liquidation — winding up isn't the same as a fire sale; a good-faith accounting and payment suffices.

Why it matters: The move from aggregate-theory dissolution to entity continuity (with Giles).

sections.title: Consequences of dissolution
sections.html:
supplemental reading

Prentiss v. Sheffel (Ariz. App. 1973)

Source: casebook p. 367 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: Two majority partners froze out a minority partner in a shopping-center partnership; the court ordered a sale and let the majority bid.

Held: Allowed — no bad-faith plan was shown, and their bid raised the price, increasing the minority partner's share.

Why it matters: How judicial sales work in winding up.

supplemental reading

Disotell v. Stiltner (Alaska 2004)

Source: casebook p. 371 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: A hotel partnership dissolved before earning any profit; the trial court let one partner buy the other out rather than sell the property.

Held: A buyout instead of liquidation is allowed, but only at fair market value proven by evidence; a partner must account for personal use of partnership property during winding up.

Why it matters: The shift from forced liquidation to buyouts (now RUPA § 701).

supplemental reading

Monin v. Monin (Ky. App. 1989)

Source: casebook p. 379 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: After agreeing to auction the partnership's assets (including a milk-hauling contract) to his brother, Sonny kept competing for the contract himself and won it.

Held: Breach of fiduciary duty; $64,000 damages. Duties continue until winding up is complete.

Why it matters: Dissolution doesn't free a partner to take the firm's key asset.

supplemental reading

Pav-Saver Corp. v. Vasso Corp. (Ill. App. 1986)

Source: casebook p. 382 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: A partner that contributed patents ended a partnership the agreement called "permanent."

Held: Wrongful dissolution: the other partner may continue the business and keep using the patents, value the wrongdoer's interest without goodwill, and collect liquidated damages.

Why it matters: The UPA's consequences for wrongful dissolution; plan for what happens to contributed property.

sections.title: XII. Loss Sharing — Kovacik v. Reed
sections.html:
main case ★

Kovacik v. Reed (Cal. 1957)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 388. Class 8 slides.

Facts: Kovacik put up $10,000 and Reed only unpaid labor for a 50/50 profit split; losses were never discussed. The venture lost $8,680, and Kovacik sued Reed for half.

Held: Reed owes nothing: where one partner contributes money and the other only services, each loses his own contribution.

Why it matters: The key loss-sharing case — an exception to UPA § 18(a) that RUPA rejects.

  • Statute (UPA § 18(a), § 40(b), (d)): losses shared like profits; capital returned before profits → Reed owes Kovacik $4,340.

Kovacik v. Reed

Kovacik

Reed

Capital contributed

$10,000

—

Loss share (statute)

$4,340

$4,340 (pays in)

Statutory result

Gets $5,660 ($1,320 + Reed's $4,340)

Out of pocket $4,340

Kovacik holding

Bears all $8,680; gets $1,320

$0 — loses only his labor

  • Holding: "Upon loss of the money the party who contributed it is not entitled to recover any part of it from the party who contributed only services." Rationale: each lost his own capital — money vs. labor; equal profit split implies equal valuation of contributions.
  • Possible rules: capital partner bears all capital losses; share capital losses like profits (statute); share in ratio of capital contributions. Concern: the Kovacik rule may make the service partner too willing to take risks.
  • Not applied if the service partner was paid a salary or made any (even nominal) capital contribution. RUPA rejects Kovacik (§ 401 comment: default loss rules apply even if a partner contributed no capital).
  • Professor's point: the parties probably wouldn't have agreed to equal loss sharing — but also probably not to zero loss for the service partner (losses often trace to the service partner's work, and Kovacik may encourage his risk-taking). A real bargain likely lands in the middle; the hypothetical-bargain model doesn't say where — so draft a loss clause.

sections.title: XIII. Buyout Agreements
sections.html:
• What: lets a partner exit for cash, payments, or assets in exchange for his interest; must be tailored.
  • Drafting checklist:
    (1) triggers (death, disability, retirement, divorce, bankruptcy, withdrawal, creditor seizure, proposed transfer);
    (2) obligation vs. option (firm or other investors) and what happens if someone refuses;
    (3) offer procedures (first mover sets the price ◆ — a "shotgun" clause);
    (4) treatment of contributed IP;
    (5) price method (book value, appraisal, formula, annual agreed price);
    (6) payment (lump sum vs. installments with interest);
    (7) protection against partnership debts.
  • Typical provisions:
    (1) list of owners and interests;
    (2) firm obligation to buy/sell;
    (3) trigger events;
    (4) price or formula;
    (5) payment terms.
  • Purposes: orderly transfer; keep control and choose new owners; pass business to the right family members; create a market for inactive owners' interests.
  • Funding: death → life insurance; retirement → pension/401(k); disability → disability insurance; divorce → plan for it (Alaska Plastics); otherwise formula; return of capital = capital account balance + unallocated profits.
main case ★

G & S Investments v. Belman (Ariz. App. 1984)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 412. Class 8 slides.

Facts: A general partner's cocaine use made him erratic and harmful to the business; he then died. The agreement let survivors continue and buy his interest for his "capital account" plus average recent profits.

Held: Suing for dissolution didn't dissolve the partnership; "capital account" means the book figure (negative here), not market value, so the estate got $4,867.57.

Why it matters: Buyout clauses are enforced as written — the danger of book-value formulas.

sections.title: XIV. Limited Partnerships, LLPs and LLLPs
sections.html:
• Unlimited liability: UPA § 15 (joint and several for torts; joint for contracts); RUPA § 306(a) (joint and several for all).
  • LP: general partners manage and have full liability; limited partners have no daily role and no liability beyond investment; both own and share profits. Old "control rule" (LP who participates in control loses shield) largely eliminated by the Uniform Limited Partnership Act (ULPA) (2001) § 303(a). Common structure: corporation as sole general partner (GP) (often for real estate). LLLP shields GPs too; LLP shields general partners by filing (RUPA §§ 306(c), 901).
  • 1980s trends driving limited liability: mega professional partnerships; repeal of professional-corporation tax benefits; mass financial torts against lawyers/accountants; Texas real estate crash; savings and loan (S&L) crisis; soaring insurance premiums; Internal Revenue Service (IRS) allowing pass-through for limited-liability entities.
slide reference ★

Frigidaire Sales Corp. v. Union Properties, Inc. (Wash. 1977)

Source: casebook p. 417 (outside the assigned pages). Class 8 slides.

Facts: Two men were limited partners of a limited partnership and also ran its only general partner, a corporation. The partnership breached a contract with Frigidaire, which sued them personally.

Held: Not personally liable. They acted only as officers of the corporate general partner, and Frigidaire knew it dealt with the corporation; the remedy for undercapitalization is veil piercing.

Why it matters: How a corporate general partner gives everyone in an LP limited liability.

supplemental reading

Jerman v. O'Leary (Ariz. App. 1985)

Source: casebook p. 419 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: General partners bought partnership land for themselves under a "sole discretion" clause, using an appraisal that ignored the land's favorable rezoning.

Held: The clause allowed the purchase but didn't end their fiduciary duties: they had to pay fair value and disclose facts bearing on value; remanded.

Why it matters: Courts may read fiduciary duties into permissive agreements (contrast Sonet).

supplemental reading

Sonet v. Plum Creek Timber Co., L.P. (Del. Ch. 1998)

Source: casebook p. 424 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: A public limited partnership's general partner proposed converting it to a real estate investment trust (REIT) and taking 27% of the new shares; a unitholder alleged unfair self-dealing.

Held: Dismissed. Under Delaware law, a clear partnership agreement displaces default fiduciary duties; this one let the general partner propose a merger subject to a two-thirds unitholder vote — "the ballot box, not the courthouse."

Why it matters: Delaware's contract-first approach to LPs.

supplemental reading

Cincinnati SMSA L.P. v. Cincinnati Bell Cellular Systems Co. (Del. 1998)

Source: casebook p. 430 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: An LP agreement barred partners from offering "cellular service," defined narrowly, but allowed other businesses. A partner started offering a newer phone service.

Held: No breach; courts won't use the implied covenant to expand a precise, unambiguous noncompete.

Why it matters: The narrow role of the implied covenant (compare Nemec).

case

In re El Paso Pipeline Partners, L.P. Derivative Litigation (Del. Ch. 2014) — contract standards replace fiduciary duties

Source: casebook p. 435 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: A parent company sold assets to the public partnership it controlled. The partnership agreement replaced fiduciary duties with approval by a conflicts committee acting in subjective good faith.

Held: That contract standard governs. The committee wasn't liable for information it never had (in a later trial on a second sale, it was found to have breached).

Why it matters: In Delaware alternative entities, investors may get only the contract's protections.

sections.title: XV. Forming an LLC
sections.html:
rule

What an LLC is (casebook p. 509; RULLCA §§ 108, 201, 301, 304)

An LLC combines the corporation's limited liability with partnership-style single-level, pass-through taxation (losses pass through to members as incurred) and flexible management. Its owners are members. It may be member-managed (like a partnership) or manager-managed (like a corporation); managers need not be members.

Entity: an LLC is an entity distinct from its members (RULLCA § 108(a)) with perpetual duration (§ 108(c)).

Formation all required: (1) one or more organizers deliver a certificate of organization to the Secretary of State for filing (§ 201(a)), stating the name, principal office and registered agent (§ 201(b)); and (2) the company is formed when the certificate becomes effective and at least one person has become a member (§ 201(d)). Delaware calls the filing a certificate of formation; it is a brief formal document, and the operating agreement supplies the deal (Elf Atochem North America).

Shield: a debt, obligation or other liability of the LLC is solely the company's; a member or manager is not personally liable for it solely by reason of being or acting as a member or manager (§ 304(a)). Failing to observe formalities is not a ground for owner liability (§ 304(b)).

No agency by status: a member is not an agent of the LLC solely by reason of being a member (§ 301(a)) — the opposite of RUPA § 301, under which every partner is an agent of the partnership. Authority comes from agency law (actual and apparent authority) and any statement of authority (§ 302).

sections.title: Dealing with third parties: disclose the LLC or be a party
sections.html:
rule

Agent liability for an unidentified (partially disclosed) principal

An agent who negotiates a contract avoids becoming a party to it only by disclosing all required: (1) that he is acting for a principal; and (2) the principal's identity. If the third party knows there is a principal but not who it is, the agent is ordinarily a party and personally liable (Water, Waste & Land; compare Atlantic Salmon A/S, Section II). Whether the principal was disclosed is a question of fact.

A statute making the filed articles notice of the company's LLC status protects members and managers only from liability based on their status. It does not displace agency law when the third party sues an agent who never identified the LLC (Water, Waste & Land).

main case

Water, Waste & Land, Inc. v. Lanham (Colo. 1998) — LLC agents who don't disclose the company

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 509–514 (d/b/a Westec).

Facts: Clark and Lanham were managers and members of Preferred Income Investors, L.L.C. Clark hired Westec for engineering work on a restaurant project and gave Westec a business card showing only the letters "P.I.I." and Lanham's address, with no sign that P.I.I. was an LLC. Westec did the work and was not paid $9,183. The county court held Lanham and the company liable; the district court reversed, relying on Colorado's provision that the filed articles are notice of LLC status.

Held: Reversed; Lanham is personally liable. Under agency law an agent is a party to a contract for a partially disclosed principal. The notice statute reaches only status-based liability; reading it to give every third party constructive notice of an undisclosed principal would invite fraud, and statutes in derogation of the common law are strictly construed. The missing link was never saying that P.I.I. meant Preferred Income Investors, LLC.

Why it matters: Forming an LLC is not enough: the people who deal for it must identify the company. The Act's name requirement ("LLC" in the name) points the same way.

  • Analysis 1 (silence): if Lanham had given no hint of any principal at all, his statutory argument would protect him even more — proof that it proves too much. The LLC would be an undisclosed principal and the agent plainly a party.
  • Analysis 2 (a principal who wants anonymity): the agent must either disclose the principal or get the third party's agreement that the agent is not a party to the contract.

sections.title: Defective formation: de facto LLC and LLC by estoppel
sections.html:
rule

Two doctrines borrowed from corporate law (Duray Development)

De facto corporation all required: the incorporators
(1) proceeded in good faith;
(2) under a valid statute;
(3) for an authorized purpose; and
(4) executed and acknowledged articles. A de facto entity is an entity against all the world except the state.

Corporation by estoppel: a third party who dealt with a body as an entity under its assumed name is estopped to deny its existence in order to reach the individuals. It is an equitable remedy between the parties and does not create the entity.

Michigan applied both to LLCs, even though its LLC Act says exactly when an LLC comes into existence.

main case

Duray Development, LLC v. Perrin (Mich. App. 2010) — de facto LLC and LLC by estoppel

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 515–521.

Facts: Duray hired Perrin and Perrin Excavating to excavate a subdivision. A month later the parties signed a superseding contract with Outlaw Excavating, LLC, which Perrin had just formed and signed for. The state did not endorse Outlaw's articles as filed until a month after that second contract. The work was late and poor; the trial court held Perrin personally liable for $96,367.68 because the Act superseded the de facto doctrine.

Held: Reversed. (1) The de facto corporation doctrine applies to LLCs: Perrin acted in good faith under a valid statute for a lawful purpose and had signed articles, so Outlaw, not Perrin, is liable on the second contract. (2) LLC by estoppel also applies: Duray dealt only with Outlaw after the second contract (bills, insurance certificate) and so cannot deny its existence.

Why it matters: A technically premature LLC can still shield its owner. Exam trap: Perrin was personally a party to the first contract; he escaped only because the parties replaced it with a contract naming the LLC.

  • Analysis 1(a): if Duray's own owner told Perrin to put off forming the LLC, estoppel would likely bar Duray from denying the entity, but not a mechanic who never dealt with Perrin as an LLC; and with no good-faith attempt to organize there is no de facto LLC.
  • Analysis 1(b): if the lawyer stopped work after initial drafts and nothing was filed until the project ended, the good-faith and executed-articles elements are doubtful; estoppel turns on how the third party dealt with the business.
  • Policy (MBCA § 2.04): the MBCA drafters tried to abolish both doctrines: everyone who purports to act for a corporation knowing there was no incorporation is jointly and severally liable. By negative inference, inactive investors and those unaware of the defect are not.
exam tips

Contract claims against LLC owners: ask, in order,
(1) did the owner sign or deal as an agent without identifying the LLC (Water, Waste & Land)?
(2) did the LLC exist yet, and if not, is there a de facto LLC or estoppel (Duray Development)?
(3) did the owner personally guarantee the debt?
(4) is there a basis to pierce the veil (Section XVII)? Status alone never creates liability (RULLCA § 304(a)).

sections.title: XVI. The Operating Agreement
sections.html:
rule

The agreement governs; the Act fills the gaps (RULLCA § 105)

The operating agreement governs relations among the members and with the company, the rights and duties of managers, the company's activities, and how the agreement is amended (§ 105(a)(1)–(4)). Where the agreement is silent, the Act governs (§ 105(b)).

It may not, among other things (§ 105(c)): alter or eliminate the duty of loyalty or care except as § 105(d) allows (c)(5); eliminate the contractual obligation of good faith and fair dealing, though it may set standards that are not manifestly unreasonable (c)(6); relieve a person from liability for bad faith, willful or intentional misconduct, or knowing violation of law (c)(7); unreasonably restrict information rights (c)(8); vary the judicial dissolution grounds of § 701(a)(4) (c)(9); or unreasonably restrict a member's right to sue under Article 8 (c)(11).

If not manifestly unreasonable, it may (§ 105(d)(3)): (A) alter or eliminate aspects of the duty of loyalty in § 409(b); (B) identify specific types or categories of activities that do not violate the duty of loyalty; (C) alter the duty of care, but not to authorize bad faith, willful misconduct or knowing violations of law; and (D) alter or eliminate any other fiduciary duty. It may also set a method for disinterested, independent persons to authorize a conflicted transaction after full disclosure (§ 105(d)(1)(A)).

Manifestly unreasonable is a question of law, judged as of the time the term was adopted; a court may strike a term only if it is readily apparent that its objective is unreasonable or it is an unreasonable means to that objective (§ 105(e)).

rule

Delaware: freedom of contract (DLLCA § 18-1101(b))

Delaware's policy is "to give the maximum effect to the principle of freedom of contract and to the enforceability of limited liability company agreements." The Delaware LLC Act was modeled on its LP Act, and a member is treated much like a limited partner (Elf Atochem North America). The Act is a flexible statute of defaults the members may change, so long as they do not contravene a mandatory provision. One protection cannot be contracted away: the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing (R & R Capital, Section XX).

sections.title: Management defaults (RULLCA § 407)
sections.html:
Issue

Member-managed (the default)

Manager-managed (only if the agreement says so)

How chosen

Default unless the agreement expressly says "manager-managed," "managed by managers" or "vested in managers," or uses words of similar import (§ 407(a))

Agreement opts in (§ 407(a)); managers chosen and removable at any time, without cause, by a majority of the members (§ 407(c)(4))

Ordinary matters

Each member has equal rights; differences decided by a majority of the members (§ 407(b)(2)–(3))

Decided exclusively by the manager or a majority of the managers (§ 407(c)(1))

Acts outside the ordinary course; amending the agreement

All members (§ 407(b)(4))

All members (§ 407(c)(3))

Fiduciary duties

Members owe loyalty and care to the company and the other members (§ 409(a))

Managers owe them; a member owes no duty solely by reason of being a member (§ 409(i)(1), (6))

Pay and advances

No pay for services except reasonable pay for winding up (§ 407(h)); an advance beyond agreed capital is a loan that bears interest (§ 407(f)–(g))

Set by the agreement

sections.title: Money, transfers and suits
sections.html:
• Distributions: before dissolution, any distribution is in equal shares among members and dissociated members (RULLCA § 404(a)) — per capita, not by contribution, unless the agreement says otherwise; there is no right to an interim distribution unless the company decides to make one, and dissociation does not entitle a person to one (§ 404(b)).
  • Limits: no distribution if afterward (1) the company could not pay its debts as they come due, or (2) its total assets would be less than its total liabilities (§ 405(a)). A member or manager who consents to an improper distribution in breach of § 409 is personally liable to the company for the excess (§ 406).
  • Transfers: a transferee of a member's transferable interest gets only distributions, not management rights; a creditor's charging order is a lien on the debtor's distributions (§§ 502–503).
  • Direct vs. derivative suits: a claim for an injury to the LLC belongs to the LLC. Tests: (1) who suffered the most immediate and direct injury, and (2) to whom did the defendant's duty run? If the answer to either is the company, the suit is derivative (casebook pp. 514–515). A direct action needs an actual or threatened injury not solely the result of an injury to the company (§ 801(b)); a derivative action needs a refused demand or a showing that demand would be futile (§ 802).
main case

Elf Atochem North America, Inc. v. Jaffari (Del. 1999) — the LLC agreement binds the LLC; forum and arbitration clauses

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 521–528.

Facts: Elf (30%, $1 million) and Jaffari's company Malek, Inc. (70%, its maskant technology) formed Malek LLC, with Jaffari as manager. The LLC agreement, which the LLC itself never signed, sent every dispute to arbitration or court in California. Elf sued Jaffari in the Delaware Court of Chancery, individually and derivatively, for breach of fiduciary duty and other wrongs.

Held: Dismissal affirmed. (1) The LLC agreement binds the LLC even though it did not sign it. (2) The Act does not forbid members from vesting exclusive jurisdiction in California arbitration, so the forum clauses govern derivative as well as direct claims. Members may contract around the Act's default grants of Chancery jurisdiction (§§ 18-110(a), 18-111, 18-1001).

Why it matters: The leading statement of Delaware's freedom-of-contract policy for LLCs: the members' agreement controls, and calling a claim derivative does not escape it.

  • Analysis 2 (a total exculpation clause): a clause relieving members of all liability "regardless of any allegation of willfulness, intention, or gross negligence" would fail under RULLCA § 105(c)(7) for bad faith, willful misconduct and knowing violations. Delaware's § 18-1101(e) lets an LLC agreement limit or eliminate liability for breach of duties but not for a bad-faith violation of the implied covenant.
  • Analysis 1 and 3: a party may accept an arbitration clause to get the deal done; Delaware sees no reason to stop sophisticated parties from choosing their forum.
rule

The implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing (Fisk Ventures)

Every contract carries an implied covenant requiring a party to refrain from arbitrary or unreasonable conduct that prevents the other party from receiving the fruits of the bargain. It all required
(1) fills a gap only where it is clear the parties would have agreed to the term had they thought to negotiate it;
(2) protects the spirit of what was actually bargained for; and
(3) cannot be invoked where the contract expressly covers the subject. The mere exercise of one's contractual rights, without more, is not a breach. Under RULLCA the obligation is contractual and cannot be eliminated (§§ 105(c)(6), 409(d)).

main case

Fisk Ventures, LLC v. Segal (Del. Ch. 2008 and 2009) — the implied covenant (2008); dissolution of a deadlocked LLC (2009)

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 528–535 (2008, aff'd sub nom. Segal v. Fisk Ventures, LLC (Del. 2009)) and pp. 617–624 (2009).

Facts: Segal founded Genitrix, LLC with patent rights (about 55% of Class A); Johnson and Fisk Ventures invested heavily (Class B). The board needed 75% approval for most actions, so neither class could act alone. Class B held a Put Right to force the company to buy its interests at appraised value, paid in secured notes if large, and refused to waive it although investors called it a deal killer. Class B also blocked Segal's financing plans. Genitrix ran out of cash and had no office, funds or revenue; Fisk sought dissolution and Segal counterclaimed.

Held: 2008: Segal's claims dismissed. The agreement gave each class rights and did not oblige one to accept the other's business judgment; requiring 75% approval for financing implied a right to block, and exercising that contractual right is no breach of the agreement or of the implied covenant. 2009: dissolution granted under DLLCA § 18-802: (1) the board was hopelessly deadlocked; (2) the agreement gave no way around the deadlock — the Put Right is Fisk's option, not a mechanism the company can use to force out an uncooperative member; and (3) the company's finances left effectively no business to run.

Why it matters: Veto rights cut both ways: they protect each side and can freeze the company. The court will not use the implied covenant to rewrite a negotiated veto, but deadlock plus no exit is the classic ground for judicial dissolution (Section XX).

  • Analysis 1 (veto power): each side wanted protection against the other; a tie-breaker (an independent director, a buy-sell "shotgun" clause, mediation or arbitration of deadlocks) would have avoided the stalemate.
  • Analysis 2 (the Put Right): it gave Class B a guaranteed exit at appraised value with priority over later investors, which is why new money insisted on its waiver and why Johnson would not give it up.
  • Analysis 3 (order more investment?): no court can make members contribute capital they never promised (compare McConnell and Racing Investment Fund 2000).

sections.title: XVII. Piercing the LLC Veil
sections.html:
rule

Veil piercing applies to LLCs

Limited liability is the rule (RULLCA § 304(a)); piercing is an equitable exception. Courts apply corporate piercing law to LLCs, by statute (Minnesota, in Tom Thumb Food Markets) or by analogy (Delaware, in NetJets Aviation).

Minnesota all required: (1) the entity ignored formalities and acted as the owner's alter ego or instrumentality; and (2) respecting limited liability would be unjust or fundamentally unfair (Tom Thumb Food Markets).

Delaware alter ego all required: (1) the entity and its owner operated as a single economic entity; and (2) an overall element of injustice or unfairness. Actual fraud is not required (NetJets Aviation).

Factors (weighed together; no single one is enough):
(a) adequate capitalization for the undertaking;
(b) solvency;
(c) whether distributions were paid, records kept and formalities observed;
(d) whether the dominant owner siphoned funds; and
(e) whether the entity was simply a facade for the owner. For an LLC, less weight goes to internal formalities because fewer are required — and RULLCA § 304(b) says failing to observe them is not itself a ground for liability.

main case

Tom Thumb Food Markets, Inc. v. TLH Properties, LLC (Minn. App. 1999, unpublished) — no piercing without injustice; clean hands

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 536–539.

Facts: Developer Hartmann told Tom Thumb he had bought land he only had an oral deal to develop, then signed a 12-year lease for his LLC, TLH, as landlord, with no financing contingency. Tom Thumb ignored the bank's requests for its financial statements; when they arrived, the bank refused to lend because Tom Thumb had a negative net worth. The land was sold to another buyer. The trial court found TLH breached and pierced the veil to hold Hartmann liable for $492,000 in lost profits.

Held: The lease had no contingency, so TLH breached. But piercing was reversed: Minnesota applies corporate piercing law to LLCs by statute, and the record showed no injustice or fundamental unfairness. Hartmann formed the LLC to build the Tom Thumb store, not to defraud, and Tom Thumb lacked clean hands because its own delay and finances caused the financing failure.

Why it matters: Misstatements and a thinly funded LLC are not enough; piercing needs injustice, and equity looks at the plaintiff's conduct too.

main case

NetJets Aviation, Inc. v. LHC Communications, LLC (2d Cir. 2008) — piercing a single-member Delaware LLC

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 539–545.

Facts: LHC, a Delaware LLC whose sole member was Zimmerman, leased a fractional airplane interest from NetJets and stopped paying. Zimmerman and his family used LHC's flight hours for personal trips, moved money between LHC and his other companies, and withdrew LHC funds at will; his payments into LHC were labeled loans so he could take money back out, leaving LHC with no assets.

Held: Summary judgment for Zimmerman vacated; NetJets gets a trial on alter-ego liability. Delaware's two-prong test applies to LLCs. A factfinder could find (1) a single economic entity — Zimmerman treated LHC's bank account as one of his pockets — and (2) an overall element of injustice, since his contributions could be found deliberately mischaracterized as loans to mask withdrawals that DLLCA § 18-607 forbids.

Why it matters: Siphoning and treating the company's account as your own, not missing minutes, is what pierces an LLC.

  • Protecting the creditor (NetJets Analysis 1): get a personal guaranty, a parent guaranty, a deposit or financial covenants up front — the cheapest way to avoid the lawsuit.
  • Protecting the owner (Analysis 3): capitalize adequately, keep company and personal funds and uses separate, document loans as loans, and take money out only through lawful distributions.
  • Formalities (Tom Thumb Analysis 3; NetJets Analysis 5): with fewer required formalities and statutes like § 304(b), commingling, siphoning and undercapitalization matter far more than minutes or meetings.

sections.title: Veil piercing in limited partnerships and LLPs (casebook note)
sections.html:
• LLPs: courts will likely extend corporate piercing to LLPs, roughly as for LLCs (In re Adelphia Communications Corp.), though cases are few.
  • LPs — the control rule: under ULPA (1916) a limited partner who took part in control became liable as a general partner. ULPA (1976) § 303(a) kept the rule but listed safe-harbor activities (§ 303(b)), such as consulting with and advising a general partner. Courts asked whether the limited partner had at least an equal voice in decisions, so as to be a general partner in effect (Mount Vernon Savings & Loan v. Partridge Associates).
  • ULPA (2001) § 303(a) ends the control rule: a limited partner is not liable for the LP's obligations solely by being or acting as a limited partner, even if it participates in management and control; § 303(b) adds that ignoring formalities is no ground for liability.
  • Corporate general partner: a corporation may be the general partner, since ULPA (2001) defines a "person" to include a corporation, so everyone in an LP can have limited liability (Frigidaire Sales, Section XIV); creditors' remedy is to pierce the corporate GP. An LLLP gives the general partner a statutory shield too. Courts have applied piercing to LPs.

sections.title: XVIII. LLC Fiduciary Duties
sections.html:
rule

Standards of conduct (RULLCA § 409)

In a member-managed LLC each member owes the company and, subject to § 801, the other members (all apply):
(1) loyalty — (A) to account for and hold as trustee any property, profit or benefit derived in the conduct or winding up of the company's activities, from use of company property, or from appropriating a company opportunity (§ 409(b)(1)); (B) to refrain from dealing with the company as or for a party with an adverse interest (§ 409(b)(2)); and (C) to refrain from competing with the company before dissolution (§ 409(b)(3));
(2) care — to refrain from grossly negligent or reckless conduct, willful or intentional misconduct, or knowing violation of law (§ 409(c)); and
(3) the contractual obligation of good faith and fair dealing (§ 409(d)).

A member does not breach merely because the conduct also furthers the member's own interest (§ 409(e)). All the members may authorize or ratify a specific act after full disclosure (§ 409(f)). Fairness to the company is a defense to an adverse-dealing claim (§ 409(g)).

In a manager-managed LLC, the loyalty, care and fairness rules apply to the managers, not the members; the noncompete lasts until winding up is completed; good faith binds managers and members; and a member owes no duty solely by reason of being a member (§ 409(i)).

The operating agreement may narrow these duties if not manifestly unreasonable (§ 105(d)(3)) but may not eliminate loyalty, care or good faith (§ 105(c)(5)–(7)).

main case

McConnell v. Hunt Sports Enterprises (Ohio App. 1999) — an operating agreement may permit members to compete

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 550–556.

Facts: Investors formed Columbus Hockey Limited, LLC (CHL) to seek an NHL franchise. When a sales-tax vote for an arena failed, Nationwide offered to build an arena and lease it to the franchise holder. Hunt, claiming to act for CHL without consulting the others, repeatedly rejected the lease. McConnell said he would take the lease himself only if Hunt would not. After Hunt's group rejected it again at a CHL meeting, McConnell's group signed in its own names, formed COLHOC, and received the franchise. CHL's agreement § 3.3 said members could engage in "any other business venture of any nature, including any venture which might be competitive with the business of the Company."

Held: (1) § 3.3 is unambiguous and let members compete with CHL for the franchise, so extrinsic evidence was properly excluded. (2) An operating agreement may limit or define the scope of members' fiduciary duties; McConnell's group breached no duty and committed no tortious interference — it acted openly, used no CHL assets, and stepped in only after Hunt refused. (3) Hunt's company breached the agreement by suing in CHL's name without the majority approval § 4.1 required, and the willful-misconduct exculpation clause did not apply (and the conduct was willful anyway).

Why it matters: Contracting around the duty of loyalty works if the clause is clear, but members still owe "utmost trust and loyalty" in everything the clause does not cover.

  • Analysis 1 (an alternative): if Hunt, with the members' approval, had nearly closed a deal and McConnell then swooped in with a better offer, a court could find a breach: § 3.3 permits a competing venture, not undermining the company's own pending deal.
  • Analysis 2 (drafting): to remove doubt, say expressly that members may compete for the very opportunity the company pursues, including an NHL franchise, and that doing so is not a breach of any duty.
main case

VGS, Inc. v. Castiel (Del. Ch. 2000) — managers acting by secret written consent breach loyalty

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 556–562.

Facts: Castiel's entity held 63.46% of Virtual Geosatellite LLC and could name and remove two of the three managers; he named himself and Quinn. Sahagen (25%) was the third manager. Sahagen persuaded Quinn to defect, and without notice to Castiel the two acted by written consent to merge the LLC into VGS, Inc., a corporation in which Sahagen's side ended up with 62.5% and Castiel's side 37.5%.

Held: The agreement let the board act by majority, and DLLCA § 18-404(d) literally permits managers to act by written consent without notice. But Sahagen and Quinn knew notice would let Castiel remove Quinn and block them; acting in secret to defeat the majority owner's bargained-for protection breached their duty of loyalty, so they get no business judgment protection. The merger is invalid and rescinded.

Why it matters: Equity polices technically authorized action: managers may not use a statutory shortcut to strip the majority of the protection the agreement gave it.

  • Analysis 1: Sahagen, the minority, bargained for a veto over mergers (§ 8.01(c)); Castiel relied instead on his power to appoint two of three managers.
  • Analysis 2–3: the court does not make Quinn a "potted plant" — he could vote against Castiel after notice. Even a sincere belief that ousting Castiel was best does not justify the secret process; the court looked only at process and did not need to reach entire fairness.
main case

Gottsacker v. Monnier (Wis. 2005) — conflicted members may vote but must deal fairly

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 562–568.

Facts: Monnier owned 50% of New Jersey LLC and brothers Paul and Gregory Gottsacker "collectively" owned 50%. After the brothers fell out, Monnier and Paul, without telling Gregory, transferred the LLC's warehouse at its original price to a new LLC owned 60/40 by themselves and sent Gregory a $22,000 check, which he did not cash. The trial court ordered the property returned.

Held: (1) "Collectively" meant the sum of the brothers' individual 25% interests, so Monnier and Paul held the needed majority; reading it to require joint voting would let one minority member deadlock the LLC without express language. (2) Under the Wisconsin act, a member with a material conflict of interest is not barred from voting, but may not willfully fail to deal fairly with the LLC or its members. Remanded for findings on fairness, and the two must account for any improper personal profit. Dissent: Paul could not act without his brother's assent.

Why it matters: A conflict does not disqualify a member from voting; the protection is a duty of fair dealing, tested after the fact.

exam tips

LLC loyalty problems:
(1) Is the LLC member- or manager-managed, so who owes the duty (§ 409(a), (i))?
(2) What does the operating agreement say — a competition clause (McConnell), a voting or consent rule (VGS, Gottsacker), an exculpation clause?
(3) Is the modification allowed (§ 105(c)–(d))?
(4) Even if the act was technically authorized, was it done secretly or unfairly (VGS, Gottsacker)? Compare Meinhard: the operating agreement is where the parties can lower the "punctilio."

sections.title: XIX. Additional Capital and Expulsion
sections.html:
rule

Contributions (RULLCA §§ 403, 407(f))

A promised contribution is not excused by the person's death, disability or other inability to perform (§ 403(a)); a person who fails to make a promised non-money contribution must, at the company's option, pay its money value (§ 403(b)); the obligation can be compromised only by all the members, and a creditor who relied on it without notice of the compromise may enforce it (§ 403(c)).

No member must contribute more than it agreed. A member who advances more is a lender: the company must reimburse the advance, which accrues interest (§ 407(f)–(g)).

A clause letting a manager call for more capital creates duties among members and the company; it is not a promise to the LLC's creditors. A member assumes personal liability for LLC debts only by agreeing to it in clear, unequivocal terms (Racing Investment Fund 2000).

main case

Racing Investment Fund 2000, LLC v. Clay Ward Agency, Inc. (Ky. 2010) — a capital-call clause is not personal liability for LLC debts

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 568–573.

Facts: A thoroughbred-racing LLC owed its insurance agency, Clay Ward, a judgment for unpaid premiums and became defunct after paying part. The operating agreement obliged investor members to contribute, pro rata, amounts the manager reasonably deemed advisable to pay expenses. The trial court held the LLC in contempt and treated the clause as letting it order a final capital call to pay the judgment.

Held: Reversed. Kentucky's act gives members immunity from LLC debts unless a member agrees in writing to be personally obligated (KRS 275.150(2)). Because that is so contrary to the purpose of an LLC, the agreement must be stated in unequivocal terms. An ordinary capital-infusion clause is not a debt-collection device a court can use to make members pay the LLC's debts.

Why it matters: Creditors who want the members' money must bargain for guaranties; the operating agreement's funding promises run to the company.

  • Analysis 1: the members were not sued because the shield protects them; the creditor's only route was to use the company's contract rights against them.
  • Analysis 2 (default remedies): the agreement let the manager notify members of a default and borrow the missing amount; a well-drafted clause adds consequences, such as diluting the defaulting member or giving contributing members a priority return.
  • Planning (the free-rider dilemma): if two of ten members refuse a $20,000 call, the eight who pay are asked to cover the shortfall and subsidize the refusers. Solutions: dilution of non-contributors, a preferred return or priority on liquidation for those who contribute, or penalty interest on member loans.

sections.title: Expulsion and dissociation (RULLCA §§ 601–603)
sections.html:
rule

Leaving and being expelled

Power to withdraw: a member may dissociate at any time, rightfully or wrongfully, by express will (§ 601(a)). Dissociation is wrongful any one suffices if (1) it breaches an express provision of the operating agreement; or (2) it occurs before winding up is complete and the member withdraws by express will, is expelled by judicial order, or (in a member-managed LLC) becomes a debtor in bankruptcy or the like (§ 602(8)), or an entity member is expelled because it willfully dissolved (§ 601(b)). A wrongful dissociator is liable for damages (§ 601(c)).

Expulsion any one suffices:
(1) as the operating agreement provides (§ 602(4));
(2) by unanimous vote of the other members on the grounds in § 602(5) (unlawful to continue with the member, transfer of the member's entire transferable interest, or a dissolved or defunct entity member); or
(3) by judicial order for (A) wrongful conduct that materially and adversely affected the company, (B) willful or persistent material breach of the agreement or of § 409 duties, or (C) conduct that makes it not reasonably practicable to carry on with the person as a member (§ 602(6)).

Effect (§ 603): management rights and future § 409 duties end, and the person keeps any transferable interest solely as a transferee. No buyout — the opposite of RUPA § 701.

main case

Walker v. Resource Development Co. (Del. Ch. 2000) — no expulsion without a contractual or legal basis

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 573–588.

Facts: Walker joined REDECO, a Delaware LLC pursuing an oil and gas concession in Moldova, promising financing connections, and signed its operating agreement as an 18% member. When negotiations with the financier collapsed, the other three members ("the three Bills") sent him a letter removing him from REDECO, citing poor performance and a supposed admission that he stood to be paid by the financier.

Held: Walker remains a member. The real reason for removal was the failed financing. The agreement allowed removal of the manager without prejudice to his ownership rights but gave no power to strip a member's interest, and nothing in Delaware law (including § 18-1104's gap-filling rules of law and equity) supplies one. The defendants could not later justify the removal by Walker's unpaid capital contributions, a ground the letter never gave.

Why it matters: LLC members' rights "begin with and typically end with" the operating agreement: if you want the power to expel or to make an interest contingent, write it in.

  • Analysis 1: the partnership agreements in Lawlis and Bohatch expressly allowed expulsion; REDECO's agreement did not.
  • Analysis 2–3: the three Bills could have bought Walker out by agreement, or, if he would not sell, sought judicial expulsion or dissolution on proper grounds, or dissolved and re-formed according to the agreement.

sections.title: XX. LLC Dissolution
sections.html:
rule

Dissolution events (RULLCA § 701)

An LLC dissolves and must wind up any one suffices on:
(1) an event the operating agreement says causes dissolution;
(2) the consent of all the members;
(3) 90 consecutive days with no members (unless a member is admitted in time);
(4) a court order, on a member's application, because (A) all or substantially all of its activities are unlawful, (B) it is not reasonably practicable to carry on its activities in conformity with the certificate and the operating agreement, or (C) the managers or controlling members (i) have acted or will act illegally or fraudulently or (ii) have acted oppressively in a way directly harmful to the applicant; or
(5) administrative dissolution (§ 701(a)). In an (a)(4)(C) case the court may order a remedy other than dissolution (§ 701(b)).

The agreement cannot vary the judicial grounds in § 701(a)(4) (§ 105(c)(9)). A member's dissociation does not dissolve the LLC.

Winding up: the company continues only to wind up (§ 702). Assets go
(1) to creditors, including members who are creditors; then
(2) to return unreturned contributions; then
(3) the surplus in proportion to the owners' rights to distributions (§ 707).

rule

Delaware judicial dissolution (DLLCA § 18-802)

On application by or for a member or manager, the Court of Chancery may decree dissolution "whenever it is not reasonably practicable to carry on the business in conformity with a limited liability company agreement." The test is reasonable practicability, not impossibility.

Circumstances courts look for (weighed together; none is required or dispositive):
(1) the members or board are deadlocked;
(2) the operating agreement gives no way around the deadlock; and
(3) the company's financial condition leaves effectively no business to operate (Fisk Ventures, 2009).

Two 50% members (Haley): by analogy to DGCL § 273, dissolution fits when all required
(1) there are two 50% owners;
(2) they are engaged in a joint venture; and
(3) they cannot agree whether to discontinue the business or how to dispose of its assets — unless the agreement's own exit mechanism is an adequate, equitable alternative.

Waiver: in Delaware, members may waive the right to seek judicial dissolution (R & R Capital). Under RULLCA they may not (§ 105(c)(9)).

main case

Haley v. Talcott (Del. Ch. 2004) — dissolving a deadlocked 50/50 LLC despite an exit clause

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 603–612.

Facts: Haley and Talcott each owned 50% of an LLC that owned the land under the Redfin Grill, which Haley ran under an employment contract with Talcott's restaurant company. After they fell out, Haley was out of the restaurant and the two were deadlocked on the LLC's future, while the restaurant paid month-to-month rent. The agreement's exit clause let a member who chose to quit be bought out at fair market value, but both agreed it would not release Haley from his personal guaranty of the LLC's mortgage.

Held: Dissolution ordered under § 18-802. Applying the DGCL § 273 framework, there were two 50% members in a joint venture who could not agree, and Haley had bargained for a continuing say, not a passive role. The exit mechanism was not an adequate remedy because it would leave Haley liable on the guaranty, so it was not equitable to force him to use it. The parties were to submit a plan to sell the property.

Why it matters: A company that is "technically functioning" can still be dissolved; a contractual exit bars dissolution only if it is a fair way out.

  • Analysis 7 and Planning: the exit clause failed because it ignored the guaranty. Talcott's lawyer could have made the exit the exclusive remedy and required release of the guaranty; Haley's could have required release or indemnity on exit.
  • Analysis 5: an auction at which both may bid follows; the bank loan must be paid off or assumed, and the order shifts bargaining power toward the member who wanted out.
main case

R & R Capital, LLC v. Buck & Doe Run Valley Farms, LLC (Del. Ch. 2008) — Delaware members may waive judicial dissolution

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 612–617.

Facts: Members of several Delaware LLCs sought dissolution or a receiver. The seven "Waiver Entities" had identical agreements in which each member accepted the agreement as its sole entitlement on dissolution and waived any right to seek a court decree of dissolution or a liquidator.

Held: The waivers are enforced and the claims dismissed. Sections 18-802, 18-803 and 18-805 are not mandatory: the Act does not say they cannot be varied and uses permissive language. Delaware's policy is freedom of contract, there are legitimate business reasons for a waiver (lenders often treat a dissolution petition as a default), and the unwaivable implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing remains as a safeguard.

Why it matters: The sharpest contrast with RULLCA § 105(c)(9). Sophisticated parties get the bargain they made.

main case

Reese v. Newman (D.C. 2016) — the court chooses between expulsion and dissolution

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 588–595.

Facts: Reese and Newman co-owned ANR Construction Management, LLC. Newman gave notice that she would withdraw and dissolve; Reese wanted Newman dissociated so she could keep the business. A jury found grounds both to dissolve the LLC and to expel Newman, and the judge ordered dissolution.

Held: Affirmed. The D.C. statute (modeled on RULLCA § 602(6)) says a person "shall be dissociated" when expelled by judicial order, but that describes the effect of an expulsion; it does not command the judge to expel. When grounds exist for both dissociation and dissolution, the trial court has discretion to choose (RULLCA § 602 cmt.).

Why it matters: Judicial expulsion and judicial dissolution are alternative remedies, and the court picks; a member who wants to keep the business has no right to force the other out.

main case

Dunbar Group, LLC v. Tignor (Va. 2004) — no dissolution once expulsion cures the problem

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 595–599.

Facts: Dunbar and Tignor each owned 50% of Xpert, which earned about $20,000 a month under a Samsung contract. Tignor commingled Xpert's funds with his other company's, froze its checking account, evicted Dunbar's principal from shared offices, and cut off his email. The chancellor expelled Tignor as a member and ordered Xpert to keep operating until the Samsung contract ended and then dissolve.

Held: Expulsion affirmed; dissolution reversed. Dissolution requires that present circumstances make it not reasonably practicable to carry on the business in conformity with the articles and operating agreement. Once Tignor was expelled and became a passive investor, the record did not show that, and the chancellor's own order to keep operating showed the business could continue.

Why it matters: Judge practicability after any expulsion. Compare Owen (dissolution ordered) and Collins (refused) in Section XI.

main case

Investcorp, L.P. v. Simpson Investment Co. (Kan. 1999) — members who withdraw to force dissolution stay members for winding up

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 599–603.

Facts: Two family branches each held 50% of a land-holding LLC and were deadlocked. Members of one branch withdrew on six months' notice, as the agreement allowed, to force dissolution; continuing the company required the remaining members' unanimous consent, and a trust aligned with the withdrawing branch stayed in. The remaining members declined to buy the withdrawing members out but refused to dissolve.

Held: The withdrawing members, whose withdrawal triggered dissolution, remain "members" during dissolution and may take part in it; the district court erred in treating them as outsiders.

Why it matters: Withdrawal can be a weapon. A better agreement would have said who controls winding up and set a buyout price and procedure.

note

Fisk Ventures (2009) is the dissolution half of the Genitrix fight; its card is in Section XVI. It supplies the three circumstances Delaware courts look for under § 18-802, and it holds that a member's own option (the Put Right) is not an exit mechanism that defeats dissolution.

exam tips

LLC breakups:
(1) Did anyone dissociate, and was it wrongful (§ 601)? Dissociation alone gives no buyout and no dissolution (§ 603).
(2) Is there a dissolution event — the agreement's events, unanimous consent, or a judicial ground (§ 701)?
(3) If judicial: is it not reasonably practicable (deadlock, no way around it, no business), or is a lesser remedy such as expulsion enough (Reese, Dunbar Group)?
(4) Does an exit clause offer an equitable alternative (Haley, Fisk Ventures)?
(5) In Delaware, did the members waive judicial dissolution (R & R Capital)?
(6) Winding up: who participates (Investcorp, L.P.) and in what order assets are paid (§ 707).

sections.html:
note
