sections.title: Using the operating agreement on the open-book part
sections.html:
1. Find the clause. Management (member- or manager-managed; who decides what, by what vote), authority limits and officers, capital contributions and calls, distributions, transfers, fiduciary modifications and competition clauses, exculpation and indemnification, withdrawal, expulsion and buyout, dissolution events, deadlock breakers, and dispute resolution.

2. If it is silent, apply the default. RULLCA governs what the agreement does not (§ 105(b)) — e.g., member-managed, equal per-capita distributions, unanimous consent for acts outside the ordinary course, no buyout on dissociation.

3. Test the clause against the limits. Is it a term the Act forbids (§ 105(c)) or one that must not be manifestly unreasonable (§ 105(d)–(e))? In Delaware, nearly everything but the implied covenant can be contracted away (Elf Atochem North America; R & R Capital).

4. Apply it to the facts and argue both sides. Ambiguous wording (Gottsacker; McConnell), technically authorized but unfair conduct (VGS), a veto that freezes the company (Fisk Ventures), an exit clause that isn't fair (Haley), and missing expulsion powers (Walker) are the professor's recurring themes.

5. Finish with the planning point. Say what the clause should have said and how a lawyer would fix it.

exam tips

Whole-course issue checklist


(1) Is there an agency, and who is the principal? Consent and control (Section I).
(2) Contract liability: actual, apparent, inherent authority, ratification, estoppel; and is the agent also liable (Sections II)?
(3) Tort liability: employee or independent contractor, scope of employment, franchisor control, apparent agency, nondelegable duties (Section III).
(4) Duties: agent's loyalty, grabbing and leaving (Sections IV, X); partners' duties (Section IX); LLC duties and the agreement's modifications (Section XVIII).
(5) Entity: is there a partnership (sharing profits as co-owners), an LLP, LP or LLC, and was it properly formed (Sections VI, XIV, XV)?
(6) Owner liability: partners' joint and several liability, LLP and LP shields, the LLC shield and veil piercing (Sections VI, XIV, XVII).
(7) Management and authority inside the entity (Sections VIII, XVI).
(8) Exit: dissociation, buyout, dissolution and winding up under the UPA, RUPA and RULLCA, and the agreement's buyout or exit terms (Sections XI–XIII, XIX–XX).

cases.name: Gorton v. Doty
cases.title: Gorton v. Doty (Idaho 1937)
cases.html:
main case ★

Gorton v. Doty (Idaho 1937)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 1. Class 1 slides.

Facts: A teacher offered her car for the football team's away game on one condition — that the coach drive it. She wasn't paid. The coach crashed and injured a player, who sued the teacher.

Held: The coach was her agent. She consented to his acting for her (the condition), he consented by driving, and naming the driver was control. No contract or payment is needed for agency. Dissent: just a friendly loan.

Why it matters: Shows how little it takes to form agency — a gratuitous favor with one condition supplied consent and control, making her liable for his driving.

cases.name: MJ & Partners Restaurant LP v. Zadikoff
cases.title: MJ & Partners Restaurant LP v. Zadikoff (N.D. Ill. 1998)
cases.html:
main case ★

MJ & Partners Restaurant LP v. Zadikoff (N.D. Ill. 1998)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 7. Class 1 slides.

Facts: Zadikoff ran Michael Jordan's Restaurant day to day (menu, prices, staff, budgets, checks) while his contracts called him an outside consultant. He secretly helped Jordan plan a competing Jordan restaurant and recruited the plaintiffs' investors and staff.

Held: Breach-of-fiduciary-duty claim survives dismissal. Agency turns on the parties' actual practices — right to control and power to bind — not on contract labels.

Why it matters: Labels like "consultant" don't decide agency; if he is an agent, he owes loyalty and can't build a competitor while managing the restaurant.

cases.name: Rose v. Giamatti
cases.title: Rose v. Giamatti (S.D. Ohio 1989)
cases.html:
main case ★

Rose v. Giamatti (S.D. Ohio 1989)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 13. Class 1 slides.

Facts: Pete Rose sued the Baseball Commissioner and Major League Baseball (MLB) to stop a gambling hearing. Federal jurisdiction depended on whether MLB (an Ohio citizen) was only a nominal party, which turned on whether the Commissioner acted as MLB's agent.

Held: Not an agent for discipline. The clubs had given the Commissioner exclusive, independent authority they couldn't control, like an arbitrator. MLB was a nominal party; removal proper.

Why it matters: No control, no agency — and someone can be an agent for some purposes but not others.

cases.name: A. Gay Jenson Farms Co. v. Cargill, Inc.
cases.title: A. Gay Jenson Farms Co. v. Cargill, Inc. (Minn. 1981)
cases.html:
main case ★

A. Gay Jenson Farms Co. v. Cargill, Inc. (Minn. 1981)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 19. Class 1 slides.

Facts: Cargill financed a small grain elevator (Warren) with a growing credit line, bought most of its grain, and also approved its major decisions, audited it, criticized its management daily, and supplied Cargill-printed forms ("needs very strong paternal guidance"). Warren collapsed owing 86 farmers $2 million for grain.

Held: Cargill was Warren's principal and owes the farmers. Its course of dealing showed (1) consent, (2) Warren acting for Cargill, and (3) de facto control (nine factors). A creditor that takes over management becomes a principal (R2d § 14O); Warren was no independent supplier (§ 14K).

Why it matters: Agency can arise without intent from a course of dealing; a lender or buyer that runs the borrower's business inherits its debts (contrast Martin v. Peyton).

cases.name: Mill Street Church of Christ v. Hogan
cases.title: Mill Street Church of Christ v. Hogan (Ky. 1990)
cases.html:
main case ★

Mill Street Church of Christ v. Hogan (Ky. 1990)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 26. Class 1 slides.

Facts: A church hired Bill to paint it. In past jobs it had let him hire his brother Sam as a helper; this time the elders privately planned a different helper but never told Bill. The work couldn't be done alone, so Bill hired Sam, who fell and broke his arm.

Held: Bill had implied actual authority to hire Sam, so Sam was the church's employee for workers' comp. Implied authority rests on the agent's reasonable understanding from the principal's past conduct and the job's needs.

Why it matters: The model implied-authority case — prior practice and necessity, not the principal's secret change of plans, controls.

cases.name: Karl Rove & Co. v. Thornburgh
cases.title: Karl Rove & Co. v. Thornburgh (5th Cir. 1994)
cases.html:
main case ★

Karl Rove & Co. v. Thornburgh (5th Cir. 1994)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 29. Class 1 slides.

Facts: Rove's firm did fundraising mail for Thornburgh's Senate campaign under a contract with his campaign committee, approved by his aide Dickman. Thornburgh signed letters, supplied donor lists and could stop the mailings. The insolvent committee left $169,732 unpaid.

Held: Thornburgh is personally liable. A member of an unincorporated association is bound by contracts he authorized, assented to, or ratified, personally or through an agent; Dickman was his controlled agent and approved the deal.

Why it matters: Shows a principal bound through his agent's assent and control as the key to finding agency despite denials.

cases.name: Lind v. Schenley Industries, Inc.
cases.title: Lind v. Schenley Industries, Inc. (3d Cir. 1960, en banc)
cases.html:
main case ★

Lind v. Schenley Industries, Inc. (3d Cir. 1960, en banc)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 37. Class 2 slides.

Facts: A vice president (VP) told newly promoted salesman Lind to see his new boss, Kaufman, about salary. Kaufman promised a 1% commission on his salesmen's sales, though only the president could set pay.

Held: Lind can recover ($37,000 verdict reinstated). By sending Lind to Kaufman and making him Lind's superior, the company held Kaufman out as its spokesman — apparent (and inherent) authority. Kaufman's lack of actual authority is irrelevant.

Why it matters: Apparent authority comes from the principal's manifestations (the position it gave the agent), not from the agent's own say-so.

cases.name: Ackerman v. Sobol Family Partnership, LLP
cases.title: Ackerman v. Sobol Family Partnership, LLP (Conn. 2010)
cases.html:
main case ★

Ackerman v. Sobol Family Partnership, LLP (Conn. 2010)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 43. Class 2 slides.

Facts: The plaintiffs' lawyer negotiated a $1.1 million global settlement, repeatedly assuring defense counsel he had authority. His client attended the mediation, conferred with him during final talks, and never limited his authority — then claimed he had none.

Held: The settlement is enforceable through apparent authority: the clients' conduct held him out, and opposing counsel reasonably believed him. Hiring a lawyer alone isn't enough; the clients' conduct was.

Why it matters: Apparent authority can come from the principal's conduct and silence, and binds even if the agent misread his instructions.

cases.name: Williams v. Dimensions Health Corporation
cases.title: Williams v. Dimensions Health Corporation (Md. 2022)
cases.html:
main case ★

Williams v. Dimensions Health Corporation (Md. 2022)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 50. Class 2 slides.

Facts: Emergency medical services (EMS) brought a crash victim to the hospital's trauma center, where an on-call independent-contractor surgeon operated, allegedly negligently. A disclaimer saying doctors aren't hospital agents was buried in a consent form the intubated patient never signed.

Held: The hospital can be vicariously liable for its apparent agent under R2d § 267: representation (holding out a trauma center with surgeons), reliance (patients look to the facility), and reasonableness. Dissent: patient's own belief required.

Why it matters: Apparent agency can make a principal liable in tort for an independent contractor; disclaimers must be meaningful.

cases.name: Watteau v. Fenwick
cases.title: Watteau v. Fenwick (Q.B. 1892)
cases.html:
main case ★

Watteau v. Fenwick (Q.B. 1892)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 58. Class 2 slides.

Facts: Brewers owned a pub but kept the former owner, Humble, as manager with his name over the door. They forbade him to buy cigars. He bought cigars on credit from a supplier who had never heard of the brewers.

Held: The brewers must pay. An undisclosed principal is liable for acts within the authority usually given to such an agent, despite secret limits.

Why it matters: No actual authority (forbidden) and no apparent authority (supplier didn't know the brewers existed) — yet liability: the classic inherent-agency-power case, replaced in R3d by § 2.06.

cases.name: Kidd v. Thomas A. Edison, Inc.
cases.title: Kidd v. Thomas A. Edison, Inc. (S.D.N.Y. 1917, L. Hand, J.)
cases.html:
main case ★

Kidd v. Thomas A. Edison, Inc. (S.D.N.Y. 1917, L. Hand, J.)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 62. Class 2 slides.

Facts: Edison's agent Fuller was told secretly to hire singers only for recitals dealers later booked. He hired singer Kidd for an unconditional tour; Edison refused to pay.

Held: Edison is bound (L. Hand). Hiring singers without such an unusual condition was within the customary scope of the job, and the limit was never communicated; choosing an agent "vouches" for him.

Why it matters: Third parties may rely on the customary scope of an agent's role; uncommunicated, unusual limits don't bind them.

cases.name: Nogales Service Center v. Atlantic Richfield Co.
cases.title: Nogales Service Center v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (Ariz. App. 1980)
cases.html:
main case ★

Nogales Service Center v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (Ariz. App. 1980)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 65. Class 2 slides.

Facts: A truck stop claimed ARCO's marketing manager promised a special fuel discount if it built a motel and restaurant; the manager could grant some discounts but not that one. The jury, instructed only on actual and apparent authority, found for ARCO.

Held: Affirmed on procedural grounds, but the court explained inherent authority (R2d § 161): a general agent can bind the principal to acts usual in his authorized dealings, even if forbidden, without any manifestation by the principal.

Why it matters: Draws the line between apparent authority (principal's manifestation) and inherent authority (from the agency relationship itself).

cases.name: Botticello v. Stefanovicz
cases.title: Botticello v. Stefanovicz (Conn. 1979)
cases.html:
main case ★

Botticello v. Stefanovicz (Conn. 1979)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 71. Class 2 slides.

Facts: A husband and wife co-owned a farm. The husband alone signed a lease with an option to buy; the buyer later found the wife was a co-owner. She had received some rent and watched improvements.

Held: The wife isn't bound. Marriage and co-ownership don't make one spouse the other's agent, and there was no ratification — she lacked full knowledge and intent, and he never claimed to act for her.

Why it matters: Agency must be proven, and you can only ratify an act done (or purportedly done) on your behalf, with full knowledge.

cases.name: Ercanbrack v. Crandall-Walker Motor Co.
cases.title: Ercanbrack v. Crandall-Walker Motor Co. (Utah 1976)
cases.html:
main case ★

Ercanbrack v. Crandall-Walker Motor Co. (Utah 1976)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 74. Class 2 slides.

Facts: A buyer signed a truck order that a salesman signed; the form said it wasn't valid unless accepted by a manager or officer, and none signed. When the price rose, the buyer argued the dealer ratified the order by not objecting.

Held: No contract. Silence can ratify only if the principal knows of the deal, and no officer knew. "Ratification of an act about which the principal knows nothing is inherently impossible."

Why it matters: Ratification requires the principal's knowledge.

cases.name: Hoddeson v. Koos Bros.
cases.title: Hoddeson v. Koos Bros. (N.J. App. Div. 1957)
cases.html:
main case ★

Hoddeson v. Koos Bros. (N.J. App. Div. 1957)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 79. Class 3 slides.

Facts: A man posing as a furniture salesman took a customer's $168.50 cash; the store had no record and said he was an impostor.

Held: No apparent authority — it must come from the store's manifestations, not the impostor's acts. But new trial on estoppel: a store must use reasonable care to keep impostors from posing as staff. Plaintiff must prove (1) the store's negligent appearance of authority, (2) her reasonable reliance, and (3) her change of position.

Why it matters: Separates apparent authority from estoppel based on the principal's carelessness plus detrimental reliance.

cases.key: Trustees of the American Federation of Musicians & Employers' Pension Fund
keys: Trustees of the American Federation of Musicians & Employers' Pension Fund
cases.name: Trustees of the American Federation of Musicians & Employers' Pension Fund v. Steven Scott Enterprises, Inc.
cases.title: Trustees of the American Federation of Musicians & Employers' Pension Fund v. Steven Scott Enterprises, Inc. (S.D.N.Y. 1999)
cases.html:
main case ★

Trustees of the American Federation of Musicians & Employers' Pension Fund v. Steven Scott Enterprises, Inc. (S.D.N.Y. 1999)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 83. Class 3 slides.

Facts: A union president who was also a pension-fund trustee signed 15 settlements with an employer saying they bound the fund, though only the fund's board could settle. The fund cashed all 15 checks sent with the agreements and never objected.

Held: The fund is bound to all 15 — by estoppel and apparent authority (until the employer learned of the board's exclusive power) and by ratification (knowledge plus accepting the money).

Why it matters: One fact pattern showing apparent authority, estoppel and ratification, and how notice of real limits ends reasonable reliance.

cases.name: Atlantic Salmon A/S v. Curran
cases.title: Atlantic Salmon A/S v. Curran (Mass. App. 1992)
cases.html:
main case ★

Atlantic Salmon A/S v. Curran (Mass. App. 1992)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 89. Class 3 slides.

Facts: Curran bought salmon on credit as an officer of "Boston International Seafood Exchange, Inc." — a corporation that didn't exist. His real company had a different name, findable only in public records.

Held: Curran is personally liable (~$255,000). An agent for a partially disclosed principal is a party to the contract; the agent must disclose the principal's identity, and the seller's ability to search records doesn't matter.

Why it matters: Applies the disclosed / unidentified / undisclosed principal rules and puts the disclosure burden on the agent.

cases.name: Humble Oil & Refining Co. v. Martin
cases.title: Humble Oil & Refining Co. v. Martin (Tex. 1949)
cases.html:
main case ★

Humble Oil & Refining Co. v. Martin (Tex. 1949)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 95. Class 3 slides.

Facts: A car left for service at a Humble-owned gas station rolled away and struck a father and his two daughters. The operator ran the station under a "commission agency" contract calling him independent.

Held: Humble is liable — the operator was its servant. Humble owned the station and products, set the hours, paid most utilities, could end the deal at will and assign him "other duties."

Why it matters: Labels don't control; an oil company keeping the right to control daily operations answers for the station's negligence (contrast Hoover).

cases.name: Hoover v. Sun Oil Co.
cases.title: Hoover v. Sun Oil Co. (Del. 1965)
cases.html:
main case ★

Hoover v. Sun Oil Co. (Del. 1965)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 97. Class 3 slides.

Facts: A fire broke out while an attendant at a Sunoco-branded station filled a customer's car. Sun owned and leased the station, supplied products, trained the dealer, and visited weekly with suggestions.

Held: Sun isn't liable — the dealer was an independent contractor. He set his own hours, hired and paid staff, bore profit and loss, and could ignore Sun's advice; control over results isn't control over daily details.

Why it matters: The counterpart to Humble: branding and advice don't make a dealer a servant.

cases.name: Murphy v. Holiday Inns, Inc.
cases.title: Murphy v. Holiday Inns, Inc. (Va. 1975)
cases.html:
main case ★

Murphy v. Holiday Inns, Inc. (Va. 1975)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 101. Class 3 slides.

Facts: A guest slipped on water from an air conditioner at a franchised Holiday Inn and sued the franchisor.

Held: No agency. The license's rules (building plans, signs, fees, inspections) aimed at system-wide uniformity; Holiday Inns had no control over daily maintenance, rates, hiring, wages, or supervision.

Why it matters: Brand standards aren't control of day-to-day operations — the basic franchise rule.

cases.name: Parker v. Domino's Pizza
cases.title: Parker v. Domino's Pizza (Fla. App. 1993)
cases.html:
main case ★

Parker v. Domino's Pizza (Fla. App. 1993)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 105. Class 3 slides.

Facts: A franchisee's pizza-delivery driver caused a crash. The franchise agreement and a "veritable bible" of a manual controlled nearly every detail, from recipes and delivery to hiring advice and audits.

Held: Summary judgment for Domino's reversed — a jury must decide whether Domino's had the right to control the franchisee's means of operation.

Why it matters: Counterpoint to Murphy: pervasive operational control can make a franchisor a principal.

cases.name: Kerl v. Rasmussen
cases.title: Kerl v. Rasmussen (Wis. 2004)
cases.html:
main case ★

Kerl v. Rasmussen (Wis. 2004)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 110. Class 3 slides.

Facts: An Arby's franchisee hired a work-release inmate, who left work and shot his ex-girlfriend and her fiancé. The victims sued Arby's for the franchisee's negligent supervision.

Held: Arby's isn't liable. A franchisor is vicariously liable only if it controls (or may control) the daily operation of the specific aspect of the business that caused the harm; Arby's had no say over hiring or supervision.

Why it matters: States today's majority franchise test and why vicarious-liability rationales weaken for franchisors.

cases.name: Miller v. McDonald's Corp.
cases.title: Miller v. McDonald's Corp. (Or. App. 1997)
cases.html:
main case ★

Miller v. McDonald's Corp. (Or. App. 1997)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 120. Class 4 slides.

Facts: A customer bit a sapphire in a Big Mac at a franchised McDonald's. McDonald's dictated exact food-handling methods; everything the customer saw said "McDonald's," and she chose it for its reputation.

Held: Jury questions on both actual agency (McDonald's controlled the food-handling that caused the injury) and apparent agency under R2d § 267 (uniform branding held the franchisee out; she relied).

Why it matters: Shows both routes to franchisor tort liability.

cases.name: Brill v. Davajon
cases.title: Brill v. Davajon (Ill. App. 1964)
cases.html:
main case ★

Brill v. Davajon (Ill. App. 1964)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 125. Class 4 slides.

Facts: A Checker cab driver, against explicit company rules, pushed a stalled car for $1 and caused a collision.

Held: Checker isn't liable. Pushing the car for his own $1 was a departure from the employer's business — outside the scope of employment.

Why it matters: A personal side errand breaks scope under the purpose prong of R2d § 228 (contrast Bushey).

cases.name: Ira S. Bushey & Sons, Inc. v. United States
cases.title: Ira S. Bushey & Sons, Inc. v. United States (2d Cir. 1968, Friendly, J.)
cases.html:
main case ★

Ira S. Bushey & Sons, Inc. v. United States (2d Cir. 1968, Friendly, J.)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 128. Class 4 slides.

Facts: A drunk Coast Guard sailor returning to his ship at night turned wheels that flooded a private drydock, which sank with the ship.

Held: The government is liable (Friendly). Though Lane had no purpose to serve his employer, an enterprise must answer for risks "characteristic of its activities"; sailors' drinking and crew crossing the drydock were foreseeable. Purely personal acts (shooting his wife's lover) would not be.

Why it matters: An enterprise-risk alternative to R2d's motive test.

cases.name: Manning v. Grimsley
cases.title: Manning v. Grimsley (1st Cir. 1981)
cases.html:
main case ★

Manning v. Grimsley (1st Cir. 1981)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 135. Class 4 slides.

Facts: An Orioles pitcher, heckled nonstop while warming up, threw a ball at the hecklers and hit a fan.

Held: Battery claim against the club goes to the jury. An employer is liable for an employee's assault responding to the plaintiff's conduct that presently interferes with his ability to do the job.

Why it matters: Intentional torts can be within scope (R2d § 228(1)(d)).

cases.name: Lamkin v. Brooks
cases.title: Lamkin v. Brooks (La. 1986)
cases.html:
main case ★

Lamkin v. Brooks (La. 1986)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 139. Class 4 slides.

Facts: A town police officer, dispatched to a complaint just outside town, came back after a drunk man threatened him and punched him, breaking his face.

Held: The town is vicariously liable (its insurer isn't, due to an intentional-acts exclusion). The attack was closely connected in time, place, and causation to his police duties, not a purely personal matter.

Why it matters: Employment-rooted violence falls within scope.

cases.name: Arguello v. Conoco, Inc.
cases.title: Arguello v. Conoco, Inc. (5th Cir. 2000)
cases.html:
main case ★

Arguello v. Conoco, Inc. (5th Cir. 2000)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 142. Class 4 slides.

Facts: Minority customers sued Conoco under civil-rights laws for racist abuse by a clerk at a Conoco-owned store and by staff at independently owned Conoco-branded stations.

Held: Branded stations weren't agents (no control of daily operations or staff). The company clerk's abuse during a sale could be within scope — jury question. Counseling her wasn't ratification.

Why it matters: Agency and scope rules apply to statutory claims; owned vs. branded outlets differ.

cases.name: Majestic Realty Associates, Inc. v. Toti Contracting Co.
cases.title: Majestic Realty Associates, Inc. v. Toti Contracting Co. (N.J. 1959)
cases.html:
main case ★

Majestic Realty Associates, Inc. v. Toti Contracting Co. (N.J. 1959)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 150. Class 4 slides.

Facts: A parking authority hired a contractor to demolish buildings in a busy downtown; the crane operator knocked a wall onto the neighbor's roof ("I goofed").

Held: The authority may be liable. Demolition in a built-up area is inherently dangerous work requiring special precautions — an exception to non-liability for independent contractors (along with retained control and hiring an incompetent contractor).

Why it matters: Shows the inherently dangerous exception and that the hirer who chooses dangerous work bears the risk.

cases.name: Anderson v. Marathon Petroleum Co.
cases.title: Anderson v. Marathon Petroleum Co. (7th Cir. 1986, Posner, J.)
cases.html:
main case ★

Anderson v. Marathon Petroleum Co. (7th Cir. 1986, Posner, J.)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 155. Class 4 slides.

Facts: A contractor's employee sandblasted Marathon's tanks for years with an inadequate hood and died of silicosis; Marathon knew and did nothing.

Held: Marathon isn't liable (Posner). Sandblasting with proper equipment isn't abnormally dangerous, and a contractor's own employees are covered by exclusive workers' comp that the principal already pays for through the contract price.

Why it matters: Explains the policy of the independent-contractor rule and why the contractor's own workers are treated differently from neighbors.

cases.name: Kleeman v. Rheingold
cases.title: Kleeman v. Rheingold (N.Y. 1993)
cases.html:
main case ★

Kleeman v. Rheingold (N.Y. 1993)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 160. Class 4 slides.

Facts: A lawyer sent malpractice papers to a process-service company days before the statute of limitations ran; the server botched service, and the claim was lost. The client sued the lawyer.

Held: The lawyer can be liable — a lawyer's duty to serve process properly is nondelegable, so hiring an independent server doesn't shift responsibility.

Why it matters: Some duties are too important to delegate (R3d § 7.06).

cases.name: Reading v. Regem
cases.title: Reading v. Regem (K.B. 1948)
cases.html:
main case ★

Reading v. Regem (K.B. 1948)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 164. Class 5 slides.

Facts: A British Army sergeant took about £20,000 to ride, in uniform, on smugglers' trucks so police wouldn't stop them. The army seized the money.

Held: The Crown keeps it. A servant who uses his position or the employer's assets as the real cause of a gain must account for it, even if the employer lost nothing.

Why it matters: Loyalty means no profiting from one's position; the remedy is disgorgement, not damages.

cases.name: General Automotive Manufacturing Co. v. Singer
cases.title: General Automotive Manufacturing Co. v. Singer (Wis. 1963)
cases.html:
main case ★

General Automotive Manufacturing Co. v. Singer (Wis. 1963)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 167. Class 5 slides.

Facts: A machine-shop general manager secretly sent orders he thought the shop couldn't fill to other shops and kept the markup ($64,088).

Held: He must disgorge the profits. As a fiduciary he had to disclose the orders and let the company decide what to do with them.

Why it matters: The agent can't decide for himself which opportunities belong to the principal — disclosure is required.

cases.name: Rash v. J.V. Intermediate, Ltd.
cases.title: Rash v. J.V. Intermediate, Ltd. (10th Cir. 2007)
cases.html:
main case ★

Rash v. J.V. Intermediate, Ltd. (10th Cir. 2007)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 172. Class 5 slides.

Facts: A division manager secretly owned a scaffolding company that won over $1 million of subcontracts he helped award, even after his employer started its own scaffolding business.

Held: Breach of fiduciary duty as a matter of law. An agent must disclose matters affecting the principal's business and can't contract with it through his own company without its full knowledge.

Why it matters: Undisclosed self-dealing is a loyalty breach; a fiduciary claim works even after the employment contract lapsed.

cases.name: Bancroft-Whitney Co. v. Glen
cases.title: Bancroft-Whitney Co. v. Glen (Cal. 1966)
cases.html:
main case ★

Bancroft-Whitney Co. v. Glen (Cal. 1966)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 176. Class 5 slides.

Facts: A law publisher's president, while still in office, helped a competitor recruit his top editors — misleading his boss about a raid, handing over salary information, and choosing whom to hire and what to offer.

Held: Breach as a matter of law; the competitor is liable too. Preparing to compete is allowed, but the nature of the preparations matters.

Why it matters: The leading "grabbing and leaving" case: plan your exit, but don't use your position to raid the principal's staff.

cases.name: Town & Country House & Home Service, Inc. v. Newbery
cases.title: Town & Country House & Home Service, Inc. v. Newbery (N.Y. 1958)
cases.html:
main case ★

Town & Country House & Home Service, Inc. v. Newbery (N.Y. 1958)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 188. Class 5 slides.

Facts: Employees of a house-cleaning service left to form a competitor and solicited only their old employer's customers, whose names it had found through costly cold calls.

Held: The former employer gets an injunction against soliciting those customers and damages, but the ex-employees may otherwise compete. The customer list was a trade secret.

Why it matters: After leaving you may compete, but not exploit confidential customer lists.

cases.name: Corroon & Black-Rutters & Roberts, Inc. v. Hosch
cases.title: Corroon & Black-Rutters & Roberts, Inc. v. Hosch (Wis. 1982)
cases.html:
main case ★

Corroon & Black-Rutters & Roberts, Inc. v. Hosch (Wis. 1982)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 191. Class 5 slides.

Facts: An insurance agent whose non-compete had expired took clients to a competitor using his old agency's widely accessible customer and expiration lists.

Held: No liability — the lists weren't trade secrets under the six-factor Restatement test (all factors must favor secrecy); insurance buyers shop around.

Why it matters: Without a non-compete or real secrecy, a departing agent may solicit former clients (contrast Town & Country).

cases.name: Fenwick v. Unemployment Compensation Commission
cases.title: Fenwick v. Unemployment Compensation Commission (N.J. 1945)
cases.html:
main case ★

Fenwick v. Unemployment Compensation Commission (N.J. 1945)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 231. Class 6 slides.

Facts: A beauty-shop owner turned his receptionist into a "partner" on paper when she asked for a raise: no capital, no control, no share of losses, same job and pay plus 20% of profits if business allowed. If she was an employee, he owed unemployment taxes.

Held: She was an employee. Weighing intent, profit and loss sharing, ownership and control, management, conduct toward others, and rights on dissolution, co-ownership was missing; her profit share was really wages.

Why it matters: A partnership label doesn't make a partnership; the wages exception defeats the profit-sharing presumption.

cases.name: Zajac v. Harris
cases.title: Zajac v. Harris (Ark. 1967)
cases.html:
main case ★

Zajac v. Harris (Ark. 1967)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 236. Class 6 slides.

Facts: An illiterate man joined a car-salvage business, put in $9,000 of his own borrowed money to buy cars, and split profits equally — even on deals the other man handled alone. The other man's books treated him as an employee.

Held: A partnership existed. His capital contribution and share of all profits showed co-ownership; one-sided bookkeeping didn't change that.

Why it matters: Contrast Fenwick: putting in capital and sharing the whole business's profits points to partnership.

cases.name: Clackamas Gastroenterology Associates, P.C. v. Wells
cases.title: Clackamas Gastroenterology Associates, P.C. v. Wells (U.S. 2003)
cases.html:
main case ★

Clackamas Gastroenterology Associates, P.C. v. Wells (U.S. 2003)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 239. Class 6 slides.

Facts: A bookkeeper sued a medical clinic under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), which covers only employers with 15+ employees; the count depended on whether its four physician-owners were "employees."

Held: Apply the common-law control test using the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's (EEOC's) six factors ((1) hiring/firing and rules; (2) supervision; (3) reporting to someone higher; (4) influence over the organization; (5) intent in agreements; (6) sharing profits, losses, liabilities). Remanded.

Why it matters: Status turns on control, not titles — owners who run the business are employers, not employees.

cases.name: Davis v. Loftus
cases.title: Davis v. Loftus (Ill. App. 2002)
cases.html:
main case ★

Davis v. Loftus (Ill. App. 2002)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 243. Class 6 slides.

Facts: Malpractice plaintiffs sued a law firm's "income partners," who got fixed salaries and bonuses, shared no profits or losses, had their small capital returned without gain, and couldn't vote.

Held: They aren't partners under the UPA, so they aren't vicariously liable.

Why it matters: Profit sharing and control define real partners; titles don't.

cases.key: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Sidley
keys: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Sidley
cases.name: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Sidley Austin Brown & Wood
cases.title: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Sidley Austin Brown & Wood (7th Cir. 2002, Posner, J.)
cases.html:
main case ★

Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Sidley Austin Brown & Wood (7th Cir. 2002, Posner, J.)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 245. Class 6 slides.

Facts: Sidley demoted 32 partners; the EEOC investigated age discrimination. A self-perpetuating executive committee controlled everything, though the 32 shared profits, had capital at risk, and were personally liable.

Held: The EEOC may pursue the coverage subpoena; partners under state law might still be "employees" for federal antidiscrimination purposes if they lack real control. Concurrence: they were bona fide partners.

Why it matters: Formal partner status vs. actual power — compare Clackamas and Davis.

cases.name: Frank v. R.A. Pickens & Son Co.
cases.title: Frank v. R.A. Pickens & Son Co. (Ark. 1978)
cases.html:
main case ★

Frank v. R.A. Pickens & Son Co. (Ark. 1978)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 253. Class 6 slides.

Facts: In a 22-member farming partnership, partners bought in at book value under an understanding that the manager could end anyone's interest at will and pay book value. The manager ended Frank's interest; Frank sued to force a liquidation.

Held: Frank was a partner, but the agreement controls; he gets book value and can't force a sale.

Why it matters: UPA rules are defaults that partners can change by agreement.

cases.name: Martin v. Peyton
cases.title: Martin v. Peyton (N.Y. 1927)
cases.html:
main case ★

Martin v. Peyton (N.Y. 1927)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 257. Class 6 slides.

Facts: Wealthy friends of a partner lent a failing brokerage $2.5 million in securities for 40% of profits (capped), with information rights, a veto over speculative deals, an option to buy in, and the partners' resignations held in escrow. A creditor sued them as partners.

Held: They were lenders, not partners. Each term was a reasonable protection for a big, risky loan; they could veto but not initiate or bind. Enough such terms together could cross the line — "a question of degree."

Why it matters: The leading lender-vs.-partner case (contrast Cargill and Kaufman-Brown).

cases.name: Kaufman-Brown Potato Co. v. Long
cases.title: Kaufman-Brown Potato Co. v. Long (9th Cir. 1950)
cases.html:
main case ★

Kaufman-Brown Potato Co. v. Long (9th Cir. 1950)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 262. Class 6 slides.

Facts: Potato distributors bought interests in growers' crops, advanced money, and agreed to split profits and losses "between the partners." When the growers went bankrupt, the distributors claimed to be creditors.

Held: They were partners, not creditors — they shared profits and losses in the venture and acted like co-owners.

Why it matters: Contrast with Martin v. Peyton: sharing losses and co-owner conduct tip toward partnership.

cases.name: Young v. Jones
cases.title: Young v. Jones (D.S.C. 1992)
cases.html:
main case ★

Young v. Jones (D.S.C. 1992)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 267. Class 6 slides.

Facts: Investors lost $550,000 relying on a fraudulent audit letter from Price Waterhouse's Bahamas firm, then sued the U.S. firm as its partner, citing its worldwide-firm advertising.

Held: No partnership in fact and none by estoppel — plaintiffs didn't see or rely on any representation that the firms were partners and extended no credit on that basis.

Why it matters: Partnership by estoppel requires a representation and reliance (UPA § 16; RUPA § 308).

cases.name: Putnam v. Shoaf
cases.title: Putnam v. Shoaf (Tenn. App. 1981)
cases.html:
main case ★

Putnam v. Shoaf (Tenn. App. 1981)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 272. Class 7 slides.

Facts: To leave a money-losing gin partnership, Mrs. Putnam paid in cash and conveyed her interest to buyers who took over the debts. Later, a bookkeeper's embezzlement was discovered and the partnership recovered $68,000 from banks; she claimed a share.

Held: She gets nothing. A partner owns an interest in the partnership, not specific assets; the claims belonged to the partnership, and she sold her whole interest.

Why it matters: Selling your partnership interest sells everything, including unknown claims.

cases.name: National Biscuit Co. v. Stroud
cases.title: National Biscuit Co. v. Stroud (N.C. 1959)
cases.html:
main case ★

National Biscuit Co. v. Stroud (N.C. 1959)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 277. Class 7 slides.

Facts: In a two-man grocery partnership, Stroud told Nabisco he wouldn't be responsible for more bread. His partner Freeman ordered more anyway.

Held: The partnership and Stroud are bound. Buying bread was ordinary business, and with two equal partners Stroud "was not, and could not be, a majority," so he couldn't restrict Freeman.

Why it matters: Partners' apparent authority binds the firm to outsiders on ordinary matters, even over a co-partner's objection.

cases.name: Summers v. Dooley
cases.title: Summers v. Dooley (Idaho 1971)
cases.html:
main case ★

Summers v. Dooley (Idaho 1971)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 280. Class 7 slides.

Facts: In a two-man trash-collection partnership, Summers hired a third worker over Dooley's objection, paid him personally, and sued for reimbursement.

Held: No reimbursement. Business differences must be decided by a majority; one of two partners isn't a majority, and Dooley never agreed.

Why it matters: The internal counterpart to National Biscuit — between partners, a dissenting half can block an expense.

cases.name: Moren ex rel. Moren v. Jax Restaurant
cases.title: Moren ex rel. Moren v. Jax Restaurant (Minn. App. 2004)
cases.html:
main case ★

Moren ex rel. Moren v. Jax Restaurant (Minn. App. 2004)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 281. Class 7 slides.

Facts: A restaurant partner, helping in the kitchen after her shift, set her toddler on the counter; he was hurt in the dough press. The partnership was sued and sought indemnity from her.

Held: The partnership is liable and can't get indemnity from her. Her conduct was in the ordinary course (even if partly personal), and the statute gives partners indemnity from the partnership, not the reverse.

Why it matters: Partnership tort liability and indemnity under RUPA §§ 305, 401(c).

cases.name: RNR Investments Ltd. Partnership v. Peoples First Community Bank
cases.title: RNR Investments Ltd. Partnership v. Peoples First Community Bank (Fla. App. 2002)
cases.html:
main case ★

RNR Investments Ltd. Partnership v. Peoples First Community Bank (Fla. App. 2002)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 284. Class 7 slides.

Facts: A limited partnership's agreement capped what its general partner could borrow without the limited partners' consent. He borrowed $990,000 from a bank that didn't know of the cap; the partnership defaulted.

Held: The partnership is bound. A partner's ordinary-course act binds the firm unless the third party knew or had notice of the lack of authority; banks needn't read partnership agreements.

Why it matters: Risk of a partner's overreach falls on the partnership; protect yourself by filing a statement of authority or notifying the lender.

cases.name: Day v. Sidley & Austin
cases.title: Day v. Sidley & Austin (D.D.C. 1975)
cases.html:
main case ★

Day v. Sidley & Austin (D.D.C. 1975)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 288. Class 7–8 slides.

Facts: A senior partner who chaired the firm's Washington office voted for a merger after being told no one would be worse off; afterward he lost sole chairmanship and the office moved. He resigned and sued.

Held: No claim. The partnership agreement gave the executive committee control of firm policy and let a majority approve the merger; fiduciary duty doesn't require disclosing internal changes that bring no profit to the others or loss to the firm.

Why it matters: Partners can contract around statutory defaults (unanimity, equal management); "bruised ego" isn't a claim.

cases.name: Meinhard v. Salmon
cases.title: Meinhard v. Salmon (N.Y. 1928, Cardozo, C.J.)
cases.html:
main case ★

Meinhard v. Salmon (N.Y. 1928, Cardozo, C.J.)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 296. Class 8 slides.

Facts: Salmon leased the Hotel Bristol for 20 years; Meinhard put up half the money for a share of profits, and Salmon managed. Near the end, the landlord offered Salmon alone a far larger, longer lease covering the hotel and neighboring lots. Salmon took it without telling Meinhard.

Held: Meinhard gets half the new lease. Co-venturers owe "the punctilio of an honor the most sensitive"; the deal grew out of the venture, so Salmon, as manager, at least had to disclose it so Meinhard could compete. Dissent: the venture had ended.

Why it matters: The foundational loyalty case — the root of the partnership-opportunity rule and a manager's duty to disclose.

cases.name: Sandvick v. LaCrosse
cases.title: Sandvick v. LaCrosse (N.D. 2008)
cases.html:
main case ★

Sandvick v. LaCrosse (N.D. 2008)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 302. Class 8 slides.

Facts: Four investors jointly bought oil leases to resell. Shortly before they expired, two of them secretly bought "top leases" on the same land effective when the originals ended.

Held: Not a partnership (a single deal, not an ongoing business), but a joint venture — and the two breached their duty of loyalty by not offering the others a share.

Why it matters: Distinguishes joint ventures from partnerships and applies Meinhard's renewal logic.

cases.name: Singer v. Singer
cases.title: Singer v. Singer (Okla. App. 1981)
cases.html:
main case ★

Singer v. Singer (Okla. App. 1981)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 308. Class 8 slides.

Facts: A family oil partnership's agreement expressly let partners compete with the partnership for their own accounts. After the family discussed buying a parcel, two partners bought it themselves.

Held: No breach — the clause allowed even "predatory" competition; only taking existing partnership assets or funds would breach.

Why it matters: Partners can contract around the duty not to take opportunities (contrast Meinhard).

cases.name: Nemec v. Shrader
cases.title: Nemec v. Shrader (Del. 2010)
cases.html:
main case ★

Nemec v. Shrader (Del. 2010)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 312. Class 8 slides.

Facts: Booz Allen could redeem retired officers' stock at book value at any time. Weeks before a $2.54 billion sale, it redeemed two retirees at about $162 a share instead of the $700+ the deal implied.

Held: No claim. The implied covenant of good faith can't override conduct the contract expressly allows, and the sale was foreseeable; fiduciary claims are displaced where a contract governs. Dissent: powers must serve a legitimate company interest.

Why it matters: Insiders are held to their bargains; the implied covenant is a narrow gap-filler.

cases.name: Bane v. Ferguson
cases.title: Bane v. Ferguson (7th Cir. 1989, Posner, J.)
cases.html:
main case ★

Bane v. Ferguson (7th Cir. 1989, Posner, J.)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 321. Class 8 slides.

Facts: A retired law partner's pension stopped when his old firm collapsed after a bad merger. He sued the managing partners for negligence.

Held: No claim. Partners owe duties to current partners, not former ones, and the business judgment rule shields mere negligence anyway.

Why it matters: Shows who is owed partner duties and how low the duty of care is.

cases.name: Second Measure, Inc. v. Kim
cases.title: Second Measure, Inc. v. Kim (N.D. Cal. 2015)
cases.html:
main case ★

Second Measure, Inc. v. Kim (N.D. Cal. 2015)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 323. Class 8 slides.

Facts: Kim says he and Babineau orally agreed to build a data business as equal partners, until Babineau locked him out, incorporated the business, and raised money.

Held: Kim's claims survive. Even after dissolution, a partner must account for partnership property and opportunities; he can't dissolve to take the business without compensating his partner.

Why it matters: Duties continue through winding up — no freeze-outs (Page v. Page).

cases.name: Meehan v. Shaughnessy
cases.title: Meehan v. Shaughnessy (Mass. 1989)
cases.html:
main case

Meehan v. Shaughnessy (Mass. 1989)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 328.

Facts: Two partners secretly planned a new firm, denied it when asked, prepared client letters on the old firm's letterhead, and rushed to sign up clients the moment they gave notice.

Held: Preparing to leave was fine, but they breached loyalty by unfairly acquiring client consents. They must prove clients would have come anyway or hold the profits from those cases in trust for the old firm.

Why it matters: The leading partner "grabbing and leaving" case.

cases.name: Gibbs v. Breed, Abbott & Morgan
cases.title: Gibbs v. Breed, Abbott & Morgan (N.Y. App. Div. 2000)
cases.html:
main case

Gibbs v. Breed, Abbott & Morgan (N.Y. App. Div. 2000)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 335.

Facts: Two departing partners gave their new firm a confidential memo of their department's staff salaries and billing rates and lined up recruits before giving notice.

Held: Breach for using confidential information and recruiting before notice; no breach for planning the move together or taking duplicate desk files.

Why it matters: Confidential information can't be used for a head start (compare Bancroft-Whitney).

cases.name: Lawlis v. Kightlinger & Gray
cases.title: Lawlis v. Kightlinger & Gray (Ind. App. 1990)
cases.html:
main case

Lawlis v. Kightlinger & Gray (Ind. App. 1990)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 341.

Facts: A law firm expelled a recovering alcoholic partner by the two-thirds vote its agreement required for no-cause expulsion.

Held: No breach. Expulsion under a negotiated no-cause clause is in good faith if nothing owed to the partner is wrongfully withheld.

Why it matters: Courts enforce "guillotine" expulsion clauses as written.

cases.name: Bohatch v. Butler & Binion
cases.title: Bohatch v. Butler & Binion (Tex. 1998)
cases.html:
main case

Bohatch v. Butler & Binion (Tex. 1998)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 347.

Facts: A new partner reported suspected overbilling by another partner; the client and firm found the bills reasonable, and the firm expelled her.

Held: No fiduciary duty not to expel a partner for reporting suspected misconduct; partners may part ways when trust breaks down. Dissent: this deters reporting.

Why it matters: The limits of partner fiduciary duties in expulsion.

cases.name: Giles v. Giles Land Co.
cases.title: Giles v. Giles Land Co. (Kan. App. 2012)
cases.html:
main case ★

Giles v. Giles Land Co. (Kan. App. 2012)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 397. Class 8 slides.

Facts: In a family farm partnership, a son threatened the others ("last man standing," "paybacks are hell"), berated his father, and stalled the business.

Held: The court expelled him (judicial dissociation) because his conduct made it not reasonably practicable to continue in partnership with him.

Why it matters: RUPA lets courts remove one partner (with a buyout) instead of dissolving the business.

cases.name: Collins v. Lewis
cases.title: Collins v. Lewis (Tex. Civ. App. 1955)
cases.html:
slide reference ★

Collins v. Lewis (Tex. Civ. App. 1955)

Source: casebook p. 359 (outside the assigned pages). Class 8 slides.

Facts: Collins financed a cafeteria partnership set to last the 30-year lease; when it lost money early, he stopped funding and sued to dissolve it.

Held: Dissolution denied — the losses came from Collins's own conduct. A partner always has the power, but not always the right, to dissolve; wrongful dissolution means damages.

Why it matters: The source of the power-vs.-right rule (RUPA § 602(a)).

cases.name: Owen v. Cohen
cases.title: Owen v. Cohen (Cal. 1941)
cases.html:
supplemental reading

Owen v. Cohen (Cal. 1941)

Source: casebook p. 355 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: In a bowling-alley partnership, one partner tried to dominate, humiliated the other, refused to work, and took money without consent.

Held: Court-ordered dissolution affirmed; persistent misconduct destroying cooperation is enough. The other partner's loan is repaid first from the sale.

Why it matters: Grounds for judicial dissolution (now RUPA § 801(4)).

cases.name: Page v. Page
cases.title: Page v. Page (Cal. 1961)
cases.html:
supplemental reading

Page v. Page (Cal. 1961)

Source: casebook p. 364 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: Two brothers' linen partnership lost money for years; once it turned profitable, the brother whose company held its debt sought to dissolve it.

Held: It was an at-will partnership, so he may dissolve — but only in good faith; he may not freeze out his brother to grab the business.

Why it matters: The good-faith limit on dissolution and how to tell at-will from term partnerships.

cases.name: Creel v. Lilly
cases.title: Creel v. Lilly (Md. 1999)
cases.html:
main case

Creel v. Lilly (Md. 1999)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 403.

Facts: After a partner died, the survivors inventoried and valued the store and paid his estate its share; the widow demanded a full liquidation sale.

Held: No forced liquidation — winding up isn't the same as a fire sale; a good-faith accounting and payment suffices.

Why it matters: The move from aggregate-theory dissolution to entity continuity (with Giles).

cases.name: Prentiss v. Sheffel
cases.title: Prentiss v. Sheffel (Ariz. App. 1973)
cases.html:
supplemental reading

Prentiss v. Sheffel (Ariz. App. 1973)

Source: casebook p. 367 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: Two majority partners froze out a minority partner in a shopping-center partnership; the court ordered a sale and let the majority bid.

Held: Allowed — no bad-faith plan was shown, and their bid raised the price, increasing the minority partner's share.

Why it matters: How judicial sales work in winding up.

cases.name: Disotell v. Stiltner
cases.title: Disotell v. Stiltner (Alaska 2004)
cases.html:
supplemental reading

Disotell v. Stiltner (Alaska 2004)

Source: casebook p. 371 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: A hotel partnership dissolved before earning any profit; the trial court let one partner buy the other out rather than sell the property.

Held: A buyout instead of liquidation is allowed, but only at fair market value proven by evidence; a partner must account for personal use of partnership property during winding up.

Why it matters: The shift from forced liquidation to buyouts (now RUPA § 701).

cases.name: Monin v. Monin
cases.title: Monin v. Monin (Ky. App. 1989)
cases.html:
supplemental reading

Monin v. Monin (Ky. App. 1989)

Source: casebook p. 379 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: After agreeing to auction the partnership's assets (including a milk-hauling contract) to his brother, Sonny kept competing for the contract himself and won it.

Held: Breach of fiduciary duty; $64,000 damages. Duties continue until winding up is complete.

Why it matters: Dissolution doesn't free a partner to take the firm's key asset.

cases.name: Pav-Saver Corp. v. Vasso Corp.
cases.title: Pav-Saver Corp. v. Vasso Corp. (Ill. App. 1986)
cases.html:
supplemental reading

Pav-Saver Corp. v. Vasso Corp. (Ill. App. 1986)

Source: casebook p. 382 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: A partner that contributed patents ended a partnership the agreement called "permanent."

Held: Wrongful dissolution: the other partner may continue the business and keep using the patents, value the wrongdoer's interest without goodwill, and collect liquidated damages.

Why it matters: The UPA's consequences for wrongful dissolution; plan for what happens to contributed property.

cases.name: Kovacik v. Reed
cases.title: Kovacik v. Reed (Cal. 1957)
cases.html:
main case ★

Kovacik v. Reed (Cal. 1957)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 388. Class 8 slides.

Facts: Kovacik put up $10,000 and Reed only unpaid labor for a 50/50 profit split; losses were never discussed. The venture lost $8,680, and Kovacik sued Reed for half.

Held: Reed owes nothing: where one partner contributes money and the other only services, each loses his own contribution.

Why it matters: The key loss-sharing case — an exception to UPA § 18(a) that RUPA rejects.

cases.name: G & S Investments v. Belman
cases.title: G & S Investments v. Belman (Ariz. App. 1984)
cases.html:
main case ★

G & S Investments v. Belman (Ariz. App. 1984)

Source: principal case, casebook p. 412. Class 8 slides.

Facts: A general partner's cocaine use made him erratic and harmful to the business; he then died. The agreement let survivors continue and buy his interest for his "capital account" plus average recent profits.

Held: Suing for dissolution didn't dissolve the partnership; "capital account" means the book figure (negative here), not market value, so the estate got $4,867.57.

Why it matters: Buyout clauses are enforced as written — the danger of book-value formulas.

cases.name: Frigidaire Sales Corp. v. Union Properties, Inc.
cases.title: Frigidaire Sales Corp. v. Union Properties, Inc. (Wash. 1977)
cases.html:
slide reference ★

Frigidaire Sales Corp. v. Union Properties, Inc. (Wash. 1977)

Source: casebook p. 417 (outside the assigned pages). Class 8 slides.

Facts: Two men were limited partners of a limited partnership and also ran its only general partner, a corporation. The partnership breached a contract with Frigidaire, which sued them personally.

Held: Not personally liable. They acted only as officers of the corporate general partner, and Frigidaire knew it dealt with the corporation; the remedy for undercapitalization is veil piercing.

Why it matters: How a corporate general partner gives everyone in an LP limited liability.

cases.name: Jerman v. O'Leary
cases.title: Jerman v. O'Leary (Ariz. App. 1985)
cases.html:
supplemental reading

Jerman v. O'Leary (Ariz. App. 1985)

Source: casebook p. 419 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: General partners bought partnership land for themselves under a "sole discretion" clause, using an appraisal that ignored the land's favorable rezoning.

Held: The clause allowed the purchase but didn't end their fiduciary duties: they had to pay fair value and disclose facts bearing on value; remanded.

Why it matters: Courts may read fiduciary duties into permissive agreements (contrast Sonet).

cases.name: Sonet v. Plum Creek Timber Co., L.P.
cases.title: Sonet v. Plum Creek Timber Co., L.P. (Del. Ch. 1998)
cases.html:
supplemental reading

Sonet v. Plum Creek Timber Co., L.P. (Del. Ch. 1998)

Source: casebook p. 424 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: A public limited partnership's general partner proposed converting it to a real estate investment trust (REIT) and taking 27% of the new shares; a unitholder alleged unfair self-dealing.

Held: Dismissed. Under Delaware law, a clear partnership agreement displaces default fiduciary duties; this one let the general partner propose a merger subject to a two-thirds unitholder vote — "the ballot box, not the courthouse."

Why it matters: Delaware's contract-first approach to LPs.

cases.name: Cincinnati SMSA L.P. v. Cincinnati Bell Cellular Systems Co.
cases.title: Cincinnati SMSA L.P. v. Cincinnati Bell Cellular Systems Co. (Del. 1998)
cases.html:
supplemental reading

Cincinnati SMSA L.P. v. Cincinnati Bell Cellular Systems Co. (Del. 1998)

Source: casebook p. 430 (outside the assigned pages).

Facts: An LP agreement barred partners from offering "cellular service," defined narrowly, but allowed other businesses. A partner started offering a newer phone service.

Held: No breach; courts won't use the implied covenant to expand a precise, unambiguous noncompete.

Why it matters: The narrow role of the implied covenant (compare Nemec).

cases.name: Water, Waste & Land, Inc. v. Lanham
cases.title: Water, Waste & Land, Inc. v. Lanham (Colo. 1998) — LLC agents who don't disclose the company
cases.html:
main case

Water, Waste & Land, Inc. v. Lanham (Colo. 1998) — LLC agents who don't disclose the company

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 509–514 (d/b/a Westec).

Facts: Clark and Lanham were managers and members of Preferred Income Investors, L.L.C. Clark hired Westec for engineering work on a restaurant project and gave Westec a business card showing only the letters "P.I.I." and Lanham's address, with no sign that P.I.I. was an LLC. Westec did the work and was not paid $9,183. The county court held Lanham and the company liable; the district court reversed, relying on Colorado's provision that the filed articles are notice of LLC status.

Held: Reversed; Lanham is personally liable. Under agency law an agent is a party to a contract for a partially disclosed principal. The notice statute reaches only status-based liability; reading it to give every third party constructive notice of an undisclosed principal would invite fraud, and statutes in derogation of the common law are strictly construed. The missing link was never saying that P.I.I. meant Preferred Income Investors, LLC.

Why it matters: Forming an LLC is not enough: the people who deal for it must identify the company. The Act's name requirement ("LLC" in the name) points the same way.

cases.name: Duray Development, LLC v. Perrin
cases.title: Duray Development, LLC v. Perrin (Mich. App. 2010) — de facto LLC and LLC by estoppel
cases.html:
main case

Duray Development, LLC v. Perrin (Mich. App. 2010) — de facto LLC and LLC by estoppel

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 515–521.

Facts: Duray hired Perrin and Perrin Excavating to excavate a subdivision. A month later the parties signed a superseding contract with Outlaw Excavating, LLC, which Perrin had just formed and signed for. The state did not endorse Outlaw's articles as filed until a month after that second contract. The work was late and poor; the trial court held Perrin personally liable for $96,367.68 because the Act superseded the de facto doctrine.

Held: Reversed. (1) The de facto corporation doctrine applies to LLCs: Perrin acted in good faith under a valid statute for a lawful purpose and had signed articles, so Outlaw, not Perrin, is liable on the second contract. (2) LLC by estoppel also applies: Duray dealt only with Outlaw after the second contract (bills, insurance certificate) and so cannot deny its existence.

Why it matters: A technically premature LLC can still shield its owner. Exam trap: Perrin was personally a party to the first contract; he escaped only because the parties replaced it with a contract naming the LLC.

cases.name: Elf Atochem North America, Inc. v. Jaffari
cases.title: Elf Atochem North America, Inc. v. Jaffari (Del. 1999) — the LLC agreement binds the LLC; forum and arbitration clauses
cases.html:
main case

Elf Atochem North America, Inc. v. Jaffari (Del. 1999) — the LLC agreement binds the LLC; forum and arbitration clauses

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 521–528.

Facts: Elf (30%, $1 million) and Jaffari's company Malek, Inc. (70%, its maskant technology) formed Malek LLC, with Jaffari as manager. The LLC agreement, which the LLC itself never signed, sent every dispute to arbitration or court in California. Elf sued Jaffari in the Delaware Court of Chancery, individually and derivatively, for breach of fiduciary duty and other wrongs.

Held: Dismissal affirmed. (1) The LLC agreement binds the LLC even though it did not sign it. (2) The Act does not forbid members from vesting exclusive jurisdiction in California arbitration, so the forum clauses govern derivative as well as direct claims. Members may contract around the Act's default grants of Chancery jurisdiction (§§ 18-110(a), 18-111, 18-1001).

Why it matters: The leading statement of Delaware's freedom-of-contract policy for LLCs: the members' agreement controls, and calling a claim derivative does not escape it.

cases.name: Fisk Ventures, LLC v. Segal
cases.title: Fisk Ventures, LLC v. Segal (Del. Ch. 2008 and 2009) — the implied covenant (2008); dissolution of a deadlocked LLC (2009)
cases.html:
main case

Fisk Ventures, LLC v. Segal (Del. Ch. 2008 and 2009) — the implied covenant (2008); dissolution of a deadlocked LLC (2009)

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 528–535 (2008, aff'd sub nom. Segal v. Fisk Ventures, LLC (Del. 2009)) and pp. 617–624 (2009).

Facts: Segal founded Genitrix, LLC with patent rights (about 55% of Class A); Johnson and Fisk Ventures invested heavily (Class B). The board needed 75% approval for most actions, so neither class could act alone. Class B held a Put Right to force the company to buy its interests at appraised value, paid in secured notes if large, and refused to waive it although investors called it a deal killer. Class B also blocked Segal's financing plans. Genitrix ran out of cash and had no office, funds or revenue; Fisk sought dissolution and Segal counterclaimed.

Held: 2008: Segal's claims dismissed. The agreement gave each class rights and did not oblige one to accept the other's business judgment; requiring 75% approval for financing implied a right to block, and exercising that contractual right is no breach of the agreement or of the implied covenant. 2009: dissolution granted under DLLCA § 18-802: (1) the board was hopelessly deadlocked; (2) the agreement gave no way around the deadlock — the Put Right is Fisk's option, not a mechanism the company can use to force out an uncooperative member; and (3) the company's finances left effectively no business to run.

Why it matters: Veto rights cut both ways: they protect each side and can freeze the company. The court will not use the implied covenant to rewrite a negotiated veto, but deadlock plus no exit is the classic ground for judicial dissolution (Section XX).

cases.name: Tom Thumb Food Markets, Inc. v. TLH Properties, LLC
cases.title: Tom Thumb Food Markets, Inc. v. TLH Properties, LLC (Minn. App. 1999, unpublished) — no piercing without injustice; clean hands
cases.html:
main case

Tom Thumb Food Markets, Inc. v. TLH Properties, LLC (Minn. App. 1999, unpublished) — no piercing without injustice; clean hands

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 536–539.

Facts: Developer Hartmann told Tom Thumb he had bought land he only had an oral deal to develop, then signed a 12-year lease for his LLC, TLH, as landlord, with no financing contingency. Tom Thumb ignored the bank's requests for its financial statements; when they arrived, the bank refused to lend because Tom Thumb had a negative net worth. The land was sold to another buyer. The trial court found TLH breached and pierced the veil to hold Hartmann liable for $492,000 in lost profits.

Held: The lease had no contingency, so TLH breached. But piercing was reversed: Minnesota applies corporate piercing law to LLCs by statute, and the record showed no injustice or fundamental unfairness. Hartmann formed the LLC to build the Tom Thumb store, not to defraud, and Tom Thumb lacked clean hands because its own delay and finances caused the financing failure.

Why it matters: Misstatements and a thinly funded LLC are not enough; piercing needs injustice, and equity looks at the plaintiff's conduct too.

cases.name: NetJets Aviation, Inc. v. LHC Communications, LLC
cases.title: NetJets Aviation, Inc. v. LHC Communications, LLC (2d Cir. 2008) — piercing a single-member Delaware LLC
cases.html:
main case

NetJets Aviation, Inc. v. LHC Communications, LLC (2d Cir. 2008) — piercing a single-member Delaware LLC

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 539–545.

Facts: LHC, a Delaware LLC whose sole member was Zimmerman, leased a fractional airplane interest from NetJets and stopped paying. Zimmerman and his family used LHC's flight hours for personal trips, moved money between LHC and his other companies, and withdrew LHC funds at will; his payments into LHC were labeled loans so he could take money back out, leaving LHC with no assets.

Held: Summary judgment for Zimmerman vacated; NetJets gets a trial on alter-ego liability. Delaware's two-prong test applies to LLCs. A factfinder could find (1) a single economic entity — Zimmerman treated LHC's bank account as one of his pockets — and (2) an overall element of injustice, since his contributions could be found deliberately mischaracterized as loans to mask withdrawals that DLLCA § 18-607 forbids.

Why it matters: Siphoning and treating the company's account as your own, not missing minutes, is what pierces an LLC.

cases.name: McConnell v. Hunt Sports Enterprises
cases.title: McConnell v. Hunt Sports Enterprises (Ohio App. 1999) — an operating agreement may permit members to compete
cases.html:
main case

McConnell v. Hunt Sports Enterprises (Ohio App. 1999) — an operating agreement may permit members to compete

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 550–556.

Facts: Investors formed Columbus Hockey Limited, LLC (CHL) to seek an NHL franchise. When a sales-tax vote for an arena failed, Nationwide offered to build an arena and lease it to the franchise holder. Hunt, claiming to act for CHL without consulting the others, repeatedly rejected the lease. McConnell said he would take the lease himself only if Hunt would not. After Hunt's group rejected it again at a CHL meeting, McConnell's group signed in its own names, formed COLHOC, and received the franchise. CHL's agreement § 3.3 said members could engage in "any other business venture of any nature, including any venture which might be competitive with the business of the Company."

Held: (1) § 3.3 is unambiguous and let members compete with CHL for the franchise, so extrinsic evidence was properly excluded. (2) An operating agreement may limit or define the scope of members' fiduciary duties; McConnell's group breached no duty and committed no tortious interference — it acted openly, used no CHL assets, and stepped in only after Hunt refused. (3) Hunt's company breached the agreement by suing in CHL's name without the majority approval § 4.1 required, and the willful-misconduct exculpation clause did not apply (and the conduct was willful anyway).

Why it matters: Contracting around the duty of loyalty works if the clause is clear, but members still owe "utmost trust and loyalty" in everything the clause does not cover.

cases.name: VGS, Inc. v. Castiel
cases.title: VGS, Inc. v. Castiel (Del. Ch. 2000) — managers acting by secret written consent breach loyalty
cases.html:
main case

VGS, Inc. v. Castiel (Del. Ch. 2000) — managers acting by secret written consent breach loyalty

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 556–562.

Facts: Castiel's entity held 63.46% of Virtual Geosatellite LLC and could name and remove two of the three managers; he named himself and Quinn. Sahagen (25%) was the third manager. Sahagen persuaded Quinn to defect, and without notice to Castiel the two acted by written consent to merge the LLC into VGS, Inc., a corporation in which Sahagen's side ended up with 62.5% and Castiel's side 37.5%.

Held: The agreement let the board act by majority, and DLLCA § 18-404(d) literally permits managers to act by written consent without notice. But Sahagen and Quinn knew notice would let Castiel remove Quinn and block them; acting in secret to defeat the majority owner's bargained-for protection breached their duty of loyalty, so they get no business judgment protection. The merger is invalid and rescinded.

Why it matters: Equity polices technically authorized action: managers may not use a statutory shortcut to strip the majority of the protection the agreement gave it.

cases.name: Gottsacker v. Monnier
cases.title: Gottsacker v. Monnier (Wis. 2005) — conflicted members may vote but must deal fairly
cases.html:
main case

Gottsacker v. Monnier (Wis. 2005) — conflicted members may vote but must deal fairly

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 562–568.

Facts: Monnier owned 50% of New Jersey LLC and brothers Paul and Gregory Gottsacker "collectively" owned 50%. After the brothers fell out, Monnier and Paul, without telling Gregory, transferred the LLC's warehouse at its original price to a new LLC owned 60/40 by themselves and sent Gregory a $22,000 check, which he did not cash. The trial court ordered the property returned.

Held: (1) "Collectively" meant the sum of the brothers' individual 25% interests, so Monnier and Paul held the needed majority; reading it to require joint voting would let one minority member deadlock the LLC without express language. (2) Under the Wisconsin act, a member with a material conflict of interest is not barred from voting, but may not willfully fail to deal fairly with the LLC or its members. Remanded for findings on fairness, and the two must account for any improper personal profit. Dissent: Paul could not act without his brother's assent.

Why it matters: A conflict does not disqualify a member from voting; the protection is a duty of fair dealing, tested after the fact.

cases.name: Racing Investment Fund 2000, LLC v. Clay Ward Agency, Inc.
cases.title: Racing Investment Fund 2000, LLC v. Clay Ward Agency, Inc. (Ky. 2010) — a capital-call clause is not personal liability for LLC debts
cases.html:
main case

Racing Investment Fund 2000, LLC v. Clay Ward Agency, Inc. (Ky. 2010) — a capital-call clause is not personal liability for LLC debts

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 568–573.

Facts: A thoroughbred-racing LLC owed its insurance agency, Clay Ward, a judgment for unpaid premiums and became defunct after paying part. The operating agreement obliged investor members to contribute, pro rata, amounts the manager reasonably deemed advisable to pay expenses. The trial court held the LLC in contempt and treated the clause as letting it order a final capital call to pay the judgment.

Held: Reversed. Kentucky's act gives members immunity from LLC debts unless a member agrees in writing to be personally obligated (KRS 275.150(2)). Because that is so contrary to the purpose of an LLC, the agreement must be stated in unequivocal terms. An ordinary capital-infusion clause is not a debt-collection device a court can use to make members pay the LLC's debts.

Why it matters: Creditors who want the members' money must bargain for guaranties; the operating agreement's funding promises run to the company.

cases.name: Walker v. Resource Development Co.
cases.title: Walker v. Resource Development Co. (Del. Ch. 2000) — no expulsion without a contractual or legal basis
cases.html:
main case

Walker v. Resource Development Co. (Del. Ch. 2000) — no expulsion without a contractual or legal basis

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 573–588.

Facts: Walker joined REDECO, a Delaware LLC pursuing an oil and gas concession in Moldova, promising financing connections, and signed its operating agreement as an 18% member. When negotiations with the financier collapsed, the other three members ("the three Bills") sent him a letter removing him from REDECO, citing poor performance and a supposed admission that he stood to be paid by the financier.

Held: Walker remains a member. The real reason for removal was the failed financing. The agreement allowed removal of the manager without prejudice to his ownership rights but gave no power to strip a member's interest, and nothing in Delaware law (including § 18-1104's gap-filling rules of law and equity) supplies one. The defendants could not later justify the removal by Walker's unpaid capital contributions, a ground the letter never gave.

Why it matters: LLC members' rights "begin with and typically end with" the operating agreement: if you want the power to expel or to make an interest contingent, write it in.

cases.name: Haley v. Talcott
cases.title: Haley v. Talcott (Del. Ch. 2004) — dissolving a deadlocked 50/50 LLC despite an exit clause
cases.html:
main case

Haley v. Talcott (Del. Ch. 2004) — dissolving a deadlocked 50/50 LLC despite an exit clause

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 603–612.

Facts: Haley and Talcott each owned 50% of an LLC that owned the land under the Redfin Grill, which Haley ran under an employment contract with Talcott's restaurant company. After they fell out, Haley was out of the restaurant and the two were deadlocked on the LLC's future, while the restaurant paid month-to-month rent. The agreement's exit clause let a member who chose to quit be bought out at fair market value, but both agreed it would not release Haley from his personal guaranty of the LLC's mortgage.

Held: Dissolution ordered under § 18-802. Applying the DGCL § 273 framework, there were two 50% members in a joint venture who could not agree, and Haley had bargained for a continuing say, not a passive role. The exit mechanism was not an adequate remedy because it would leave Haley liable on the guaranty, so it was not equitable to force him to use it. The parties were to submit a plan to sell the property.

Why it matters: A company that is "technically functioning" can still be dissolved; a contractual exit bars dissolution only if it is a fair way out.

cases.name: R & R Capital, LLC v. Buck & Doe Run Valley Farms, LLC
cases.title: R & R Capital, LLC v. Buck & Doe Run Valley Farms, LLC (Del. Ch. 2008) — Delaware members may waive judicial dissolution
cases.html:
main case

R & R Capital, LLC v. Buck & Doe Run Valley Farms, LLC (Del. Ch. 2008) — Delaware members may waive judicial dissolution

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 612–617.

Facts: Members of several Delaware LLCs sought dissolution or a receiver. The seven "Waiver Entities" had identical agreements in which each member accepted the agreement as its sole entitlement on dissolution and waived any right to seek a court decree of dissolution or a liquidator.

Held: The waivers are enforced and the claims dismissed. Sections 18-802, 18-803 and 18-805 are not mandatory: the Act does not say they cannot be varied and uses permissive language. Delaware's policy is freedom of contract, there are legitimate business reasons for a waiver (lenders often treat a dissolution petition as a default), and the unwaivable implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing remains as a safeguard.

Why it matters: The sharpest contrast with RULLCA § 105(c)(9). Sophisticated parties get the bargain they made.

cases.name: Reese v. Newman
cases.title: Reese v. Newman (D.C. 2016) — the court chooses between expulsion and dissolution
cases.html:
main case

Reese v. Newman (D.C. 2016) — the court chooses between expulsion and dissolution

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 588–595.

Facts: Reese and Newman co-owned ANR Construction Management, LLC. Newman gave notice that she would withdraw and dissolve; Reese wanted Newman dissociated so she could keep the business. A jury found grounds both to dissolve the LLC and to expel Newman, and the judge ordered dissolution.

Held: Affirmed. The D.C. statute (modeled on RULLCA § 602(6)) says a person "shall be dissociated" when expelled by judicial order, but that describes the effect of an expulsion; it does not command the judge to expel. When grounds exist for both dissociation and dissolution, the trial court has discretion to choose (RULLCA § 602 cmt.).

Why it matters: Judicial expulsion and judicial dissolution are alternative remedies, and the court picks; a member who wants to keep the business has no right to force the other out.

cases.name: Dunbar Group, LLC v. Tignor
cases.title: Dunbar Group, LLC v. Tignor (Va. 2004) — no dissolution once expulsion cures the problem
cases.html:
main case

Dunbar Group, LLC v. Tignor (Va. 2004) — no dissolution once expulsion cures the problem

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 595–599.

Facts: Dunbar and Tignor each owned 50% of Xpert, which earned about $20,000 a month under a Samsung contract. Tignor commingled Xpert's funds with his other company's, froze its checking account, evicted Dunbar's principal from shared offices, and cut off his email. The chancellor expelled Tignor as a member and ordered Xpert to keep operating until the Samsung contract ended and then dissolve.

Held: Expulsion affirmed; dissolution reversed. Dissolution requires that present circumstances make it not reasonably practicable to carry on the business in conformity with the articles and operating agreement. Once Tignor was expelled and became a passive investor, the record did not show that, and the chancellor's own order to keep operating showed the business could continue.

Why it matters: Judge practicability after any expulsion. Compare Owen (dissolution ordered) and Collins (refused) in Section XI.

cases.name: Investcorp, L.P. v. Simpson Investment Co.
cases.title: Investcorp, L.P. v. Simpson Investment Co. (Kan. 1999) — members who withdraw to force dissolution stay members for winding up
cases.html:
main case

Investcorp, L.P. v. Simpson Investment Co. (Kan. 1999) — members who withdraw to force dissolution stay members for winding up

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 599–603.

Facts: Two family branches each held 50% of a land-holding LLC and were deadlocked. Members of one branch withdrew on six months' notice, as the agreement allowed, to force dissolution; continuing the company required the remaining members' unanimous consent, and a trust aligned with the withdrawing branch stayed in. The remaining members declined to buy the withdrawing members out but refused to dissolve.

Held: The withdrawing members, whose withdrawal triggered dissolution, remain "members" during dissolution and may take part in it; the district court erred in treating them as outsiders.

Why it matters: Withdrawal can be a weapon. A better agreement would have said who controls winding up and set a buyout price and procedure.
